title: UK to pay 'participation' fee to deliver EU deals
text:
The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.

The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.

It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.

Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.

Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

According to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.

The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.

This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.

But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.

The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.

However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.

Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer".

It comes as the government published separate legislation granting it broad powers to incorporate new EU laws required to implement the agreements, without having to hold a full vote each time.

The food standards deal in particular will mean Britain will have to align with scores of current EU food-related laws that have been updated since Brexit, along with future rules in these areas.

The government argues the new powers are required because it would be impractical to run a full parliamentary process each time UK legislation needs to be updated to make the agreement work.

But it has prompted criticism from opposition parties, because the UK no longer has voting rights at the EU to shape European legislation.

The government argues the UK will get a say on new rules, with the treaty texts confirming British experts can be consulted when new EU laws are being drawn up, with the UK granted "observer" status in certain meetings.

But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was showing "disdain for the democratic process" by asking for a "blank cheque to install and enact EU law".

"The prime minister is telling MPs to hand him extraordinary powers whilst having no idea what the EU will actually agree to," she added.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has argued the Burnham's deals would take Britain back into "much of the European Union's single market".

He added: "European economies are not growing as fast as ours. The idea that getting closer to the EU will mean growth for us is a myth."

title: Asia made a big AI bet on Nvidia. What happens now?
text:
Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world.

Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology.

Tech-heavy stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan went on a rollercoaster ride this week. Markets soared after a near-trillion dollar surge in Nvidia's share price but then slumped as concerns about political and regulatory scrutiny hit investor confidence.

The chipmaker is a "symbolic bellwether" of the AI trade that is fast becoming key to places like South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia," says Dylan Loh, an international studies lecturer at Nanyang Technological University.

From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes.

In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist.

That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one.

For one, Nvidia was able to grow rapidly by outsourcing chip production instead of having to spend heavily to build its own manufacturing plants.

It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC.

That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ.

"The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports".

Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island.

To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors.

On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain.

It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics.

"Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says.

In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to property services firm CBRE , external . The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025.

In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".

The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States.

But in a timely example of the importance of AI to this region, Singapore this week further raised its growth forecast for this year as the technology boosts its economy.

The world's biggest tech firms - Google, Microsoft, Oracle - also plan to boost their spending on infrastructure in the region by roughly 60% this year, CBRE added.

The demand for neoclouds, which are specialised data centres which power AI, has also risen rapidly, it said.

For economies betting heavily on AI, Nvidia has become "hugely important", with vast sums being spent on its chips and factory activity increasingly dependent on its technology, Loh told the BBC.

In many economies, news of Huang's return to Nvidia was met with jubilation.

In Taiwan, where he was born and the home of "Jensanity", investors jokingly described his return as a "one man saves the village" story.

Social media and groups on messaging platform Line saw posts like "Old Huang is back," while some investors said "Daddy is back to save my life" and "the humanitarian corridor is open."

However, some said the episode should also prompt a closer look at how effective Taiwan has been in building a "non-China" semiconductor supply chain, and how risks from the industry's heavy reliance on Nvidia should be managed better.

Asia's technology industry has been under increasing pressure from the US in recent years. The administrations of both Joe Biden and Donald Trump have tightened rules on the export of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China.

Those efforts seem to have been renewed. Just last week, Washington announced new rules that will increase scrutiny of data centre operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil.

The latest move not only restricts the export of high-end chips to China, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train AI models.

This will hit South East Asian countries, which have invested billions in data centre infrastructure to cater to Chinese firms. Nvidia has already paused shipments to the region, according to the Financial Times, although it is unclear if this is only a temporary move while it figures out how to comply with the new export rules.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a BBC request for comment.

Then there is the growing bipartisan backlash against President Trump and Nvidia after he said he "made the deal" to "convince" the company‘s board to reinstate Huang.…

title: Israeli strikes kill 16 schoolchildren so far this month, Gaza ministry says
author: Seham Tantesh in Gaza and Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem
text:
Statement follows death of sisters, aged 15 and 13, in airstrike on residential apartment in Gaza City

Israeli strikes have killed at least 16 schoolchildren in Gaza since the start of November, as young people across the territory face intensifying bombardment and struggle to find food, clean water and shelter.

On Wednesday, Gaza’s ministry of education said: “Palestinian students had been targeted for the third time in less than 24 hours, in an escalation reflecting the continued Israeli violations against children in the Gaza Strip.”

“The number of schoolchildren killed since the beginning of November has now risen to 16,” it added.

The statement follows the death of two sisters, Yusra, 15, and Jana Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 13, in the early hours of Wednesday in an airstrike targeting a residential apartment in western Gaza City.

Yusra was a pupil at Kafr Qasim school, while her sister Jana attended al-Manar private school.

The ministry added: “The girls’ father, Mohammed Majed Abu Al-Ouf, and their mother, Noura Ezzat Abu Al-Ouf, were also killed in the strike which injured several other Palestinians.” The father was a director of internal security services for Hamas in northern Gaza.

Earlier this year, an independent UN inquiry found that Israel continued to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.

On 6 November, Mohammed Nidal Barbakh, 15, was shot by Israeli forces in the Bir 19 area of al-Mawasi, Khan Younis, and later died from his injuries.

He was in the 10th grade at the Muscat school and dreamed of becoming a professional football player.

“That day, after lunch, Mohammed went to the sports academy at 1.30pm to take part in training,” his father, Dr Nidal Mohammed Barbakh, said. “An Israeli tank had advanced and positioned itself on a nearby hill before firing two rounds towards the pitch. One of them ricocheted after hitting a metal object, striking Mohammed in the back and exiting through his neck.

“He was talented and an excellent student. He was killed at the age of 15, on a sports pitch in al-Mawasi, an area where people had been told to go because it was considered safe. I do not absolve the Israeli army of responsibility for what happened. It kills every ambition within us and buries our children’s dreams before they have a chance to come true.”

On 13 November, Israeli artillery shelling killed three people in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza, including a father and his 12-year-old son, Ahmed Abu Daher, as well as a woman.

Ahmed dreamed of becoming an Arabic language teacher, like his grandfather Saleh, said his mother, Walaa Abu Daher.

“That day, my husband was heading to a condolence gathering in the al-Qastal area, east of Deir al-Balah,” Daher said. “Ahmed asked his father if he could accompany him. While they were at the gathering, they were targeted by Israeli artillery fire. Ahmed ran to ask the people attending the gathering for help. He then rushed back towards his father when a second shell was fired. Shrapnel struck Ahmed in his legs, abdomen and head.

“I cannot describe how deeply their loss has affected me. I feel as though my life stopped that day,” she added.

The Israel Defense Forces have been approached for comment.

Thousands of school-age children and hundreds of education workers have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza, while tens of thousands of children have been unable to attend school regularly.

On Thursday, Israeli attacks killed at least nine Palestinians across Gaza, including Khaled Abu Nada, the undersecretary of Gaza’s ministry of education, and his wife, according to health officials, as attacks continued despite the ceasefire in the territory.

A few days ago, the ministry of education said Israel’s attacks against students, civilian leaders and teachers were “part of a systematic assault on the Palestinian education system”.

According to Unicef , 98% of school buildings in Gaza have sustained damage, with more than 93% requiring major rehabilitation or full reconstruction, while approximately 81% were directly hit.

Young Palestinians in Gaza face a fourth winter in overcrowded tents and makeshift shelters, with limited access to basic services as the humanitarian and public health crisis deepens.

Children and young people are among those most vulnerable to meningitis, for which Gaza’s health ministry issued an epidemic alert on Tuesday after a sharp rise in infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.

Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid.

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s war in Gaza over the last three years, according to the territory’s health ministry. More than 20,000 children have been reported killed by Israeli strikes.

Éric Cantona: ‘If I regret something about the kung fu kick, it’s that I would love to kick him in another place’
author: Donald McRae
text:
Before the release of a new documentary, the unrepentant Manchester United icon reflects on his deep bond with English football and his darker instincts

“I ’m an angel and a demon,” Éric Cantona says intently during a gripping new documentary about his life on and off the football pitch. “And an angel or a demon, you love him or you hate him. I’m far from being the person with the greatest integrity. I’m far from being the person who always tells the truth. I’m far from being the person who has never been hypocritical. Maybe I’m a good person, but I can also be a flower of evil. It’s the first time in my life I’ve realised this. I am a flower of evil, and I find it very beautiful.”

It’s hard to know what to expect from the only written interview pinned to the release of Cantona: Flower of Evil . Joel Cantona has warned that his famous brother will walk out at any mention of the enduring crisis surrounding Manchester United , whether it’s a question about Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival or the Glazer family’s ruinous ownership of the club.

I prepare for a possible meltdown because rare archive footage, which opens the documentary, captures a televised standoff between Cantona and a few French journalists. He objects to the fact that L’Équipe had described his kung fu kick against a Crystal Palace supporter in 1995 as “unforgivable”. After asking who is truly “unforgivable”, and highlighting the historical sins of the Catholic church, Cantona sneers: “I piss on the pope’s arse. Just as I piss on the arse of certain journalists … including you and you,” he says, pointing to two outraged writers.

Now, 30 years later, Cantona emerges in his home city of Marseille , wearing a natty trilby. Within minutes I can tell that the flower of evil is elsewhere because Cantona is in a generous mood. As he recalls that bitterly sensational clash with the French reporters he smiles: “I’m a good client for the journalists – and they are a good client for me to express myself. We play a bit like the cat and the mouse. Sometimes we have good relationships, sometimes a bad relationship. But it’s always interesting and exciting.”

This might be Cantona at his most angelic, stretching the truth about the supposed thrill of his journalistic encounters, but it’s fitting that the film starts with the 60-year-old quoting Charles Baudelaire, the 19th-century French poet who, in his Flowers of Evil collection, wrote: “I am the wound and the knife/I am the blow and the cheek/ … The victim and the executioner …”

Cantona’s brilliance and spite defined his troubled time at six French clubs between 1983 and 1992. He could have “disappeared” from football because, despite being France’s most gifted player, he had fallen out with the national manager. The young Cantona said: “I hope people realise Henri Michel is one of the most incompetent coaches in world football.”

Michel Platini, who replaced Michel, persuaded Cantona to end his fleeting retirement in 1992 by moving to England. As Cantona says: “I knew it will be my last chance … and it’s really in England where I regain this passion for football … it’s a rebirth.”

The documentary provides a compelling account of his turbulent love affair with English football – but ignores a strange prelude at Sheffield Wednesday. Cantona tells me this forgotten strand of his story with amused incredulity. “I arrived at Sheffield Wednesday and we played a friendly. We won 4-3 and I scored three goals. And then I waited to sign the contract. At the end of the week they said: ‘You have to spend one more week on trial.’ I said: ‘No. I leave.’”

Who managed Wednesday then? “Trevor Francis – who was a great player,” Cantona replies. “Howard Wilkinson heard about that and asked me to come to Leeds. I arrived in Leeds and then we became champions and it was a great time.”

That deceptively simple last sentence fails to capture the seismic impact Cantona had on English football and especially on Leeds, who won the league title for the first time in 18 years in 1992. “It was old-fashioned football,” Cantona says. “It was interesting. There was also, for me, the feeling of adding something different.”

Was it disheartening playing antiquated football? “No, because I played with wonderful players. We had a great midfield with Gary Speed, David Batty, Gary McAllister and Gordon Strachan. And quickly [the following season] I arrive at Manchester United with Alex Ferguson. The club had the Busby Babes. That was wonderful football. Manchester United has always been a club where winning in a good way is important.”

This should be the moment to ask Cantona about the contrast with the current moribund state of United but, rather than falling out over his refusal to discuss the club now, it’s enough to hear him in full flow. “This club always loved people with different personalities. They loved George Best, Brian McClair, [Norman] Whiteside, [Roy] Keane …”

Cantona was adored at Old Trafford, as he had been at Leeds before his shock departure to United for a mere £1m in November 1992. He also led United to their first Premier League title, in 1993, after a 26-year drought.

There are great clubs in Italy, Spain and Germany so could he have resurrected his career in one of these countries? Cantona shakes his head: “I love Italian football. I love Spanish football. I love Barcelona. But nothing can compare to English football and the fans, the way they sing and express themselves. It’s so powerful.”

Cantona remembers that, when he arrived in England, “in the street, nobody knew me. I felt free for the first time in my life. I could go have a drink somewhere, listen to some music and it was always peaceful.”

Ferguson recalls that he asked Guy Roux , the wise old manager who nurtured Cantona at his first club, Auxerre, how to harness his volatile talent. Roux offered two words: “Love him.”…

title: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat
text:
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the USA is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

However, the most interesting spot to focus on is closer to home for Trump. Over half of Canada tariffs are authorised under "Section 338" of the 1930s Smoot-Hawley act. There is already a Senate Bill to repeal them, and it is possible that there would be enough rebel Republicans in the House and Senate to threaten to over-ride any Presidential veto. The incoming Senate Finance Committee chair Ron Wyden last week said Democrats were focussed on "figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto".

Before that an interim deal is being sought, and Democrat senators such as Chris Coons are appearing on Canadian TV, telling CBC , external : "Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal."

The rest of world is watching the machinations in Washington and also looking beyond Donald Trump's tenure.

It pays to look at how the initial Trump trade-quake has reshaped the pattern of world trade already.

The rest of the world has rerouted its trade flows around Donald Trump's tariff wall, proving far more resilient than expected. In cash terms, China's exports so far in 2026 are down about 8% on 2024, but that is more than 25 times made up for by its increased exports to everywhere else.

Canada has seen flat exports to the USA since tariffs, fewer cars and lumber, but pricier flows of energy. Its exports, especially commodities, to the rest of the world have rocketed.

This means that next month's G20 summit at the president's Miami resort is an important moment. In general US allies have not rocked the boat, accepting the lower level of tariffs as part of the new reality. Could the middle powers choose to upset their host in Florida next month?

The bigger question however, is how much the Democrats decide to keep of the America First trade agenda. It will not be all, but nor will it be nothing. Economists now expect some of these tariffs to stay in place for years.

title: Oxford museum displays seized belongings of Naga freedom fighter Gaidinliu for first time
author: David Batty
text:
Notebooks, clothes and ritual objects taken by British forces in India in the 1930s go on show at Pitt Rivers Museum

In 1932, British forces in north-east India imprisoned a 17-year-old girl called Gaidinliu for leading an uprising against colonial rule. While pursuing the freedom fighter through hills and valleys in the homeland of the Naga people, colonial officers also seized some of her most treasured possessions.

They were sent to the University of Oxford’s Pitt Rivers Museum and kept in storage. Now, for the first time, the museum is exhibiting the collection of 27 items, including a basket of Gaidinliu’s notebooks believed to contain her prophetic visions as the leader of a Naga Indigenous religion, clothes, bracelets and amulets.

Also on display are protective ritual objects, taken by the British from Gaidinliu’s hiding places, which they believed she had used against them. These are a stick with a monkey skull used to ward off evil spirits, and small wooden clubs, traditionally used by Naga people to cast an omen on an enemy.

The exhibition, The Afterlives of Captured Objects , raises questions about the colonial extraction of artefacts from Indigenous communities, which were often originally catalogued using prejudiced and discriminatory language, according to the curator, Clare Harris, a professor of visual anthropology.

For example, Harris said Gaidinliu’s notebooks were derided as “meaningless scribbling” by the colonial anthropologist JP Mills, who collected them. But he also recorded that these writings “gave her immense prestige”, which suggests that they may have been seized as part of British efforts to suppress the religious and political movement that Gaidinliu led, called Heraka.

While most of the objects on display were taken by the British after Gaidinliu abandoned them while on the run, two items were more violently extracted. Textiles displayed on mannequins in the show were taken from a pair of male and female sacred clay figures from a Heraka temple in the village of Kambiron in 1931.

The textiles are shown along with a photograph taken by a British officer of another soldier kneeling with the sacred figures, which were destroyed along with the temple.

“By showing the photograph at the same time, you can make the equation visually about what was extracted by the British there,” said Harris. “The British destroy the temple and they destroy the figures, so they take away the potency of those things.”

The show follows a four-year project by researchers from India and the Universities of Edinburgh and Oxford to digitise the Gaidinliu collection and share it with Naga communities in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur. Their craftspeople have used the images to revive and revitalise traditional crafts such as basket weaving and textile making, with some of their creations included in the exhibition.

Arkotong Longkumer, a professor of anthropology and modern Asia at the school of divinity, University of Edinburgh, who co-led the project with Harris, said attempts were also being made to translate Gaidinliu’s notebooks in an effort to reconstruct a new Indigenous language for the Naga people.

He said: “There are some symbols which are recognisable within stories and myths. They may be untranslatable in a conventional sense but they are being used to try and construct a language system.”

The exhibition also aims to raise international recognition of Gaidinliu, who has long been revered as an important leader in the resistance movement that led to Indian independence. After her release from prison in 1947, she became head of a political movement advocating for recognition of a Naga homeland.

Alila Chang, one of Gaidinliu’s grandnieces, said her family felt a deep sense of pride about the exhibition. She said: “These objects are connected to our family’s history and the struggles and sacrifices of our people as well. We want the world to know her struggles and for what reason she fought.”

Chang, who has come to Oxford for the exhibition’s private view, also shared a more personal recollection of Gaidinliu as a “very affectionate grandmother”.

“I remember [her] giving us sweets,” she said, adding how Gaidinliu, who died in 1993, would pray for her and her sibling when they went to school in the morning.

“She will always be in our hearts, but I think she belongs to the world now.”

title: Some old-school advice for Burnham: boost competition if you want growth | Nils Pratley
author: Nils Pratley
text:
Two former Treasury officials say the value of competition and disruption has become ‘the blind spot of UK economic policy’

T he defenestration of Marcus Bokkerink in the Keir Starmer-Rachel Reeves era is half-forgotten now – but the saga was a big deal in January 2025 and should still matter to those at the top of today’s government.

Bokkerink was chair of the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) until he was turfed out because, it seemed, he was deemed insufficiently aligned with the Starmer-Reeves idea that regulators should “support growth”. Bokkerink hit back by warning of the dangers of political interference and competition authorities becoming “vulnerable to short-term expediency or vested interests”.

The exchange pointed to a philosophical divide. Did the government see a tension between growth and competition? Was it worried that business investment would suffer if the competition regulator was too active?

One piece of context was the epic whine by a senior Microsoft executive about the “darkest day in our four decades in Britain” after the CMA – entirely reasonably in this column’s view at the time – gave a thumbs-down in 2023 to his company’s planned $69bn (£53bn) takeover of the video games firm Activision Blizzard.

Those events are chewed over in a punchy paper this week from two former senior Treasury officials of yesteryear, John Kingman and Shriti Vadera (the latter was also a minister in Gordon Brown’s government). Top lines: strong competition is unambiguously good for growth; we need new firms to break through and make the economy more productive. The problem is that the value of competition and disruption has become “the blind spot of current UK economic policy”, the paper says.

Fair point. About 60% of the fall in the UK’s productivity rate since 2007 can be attributed to less dynamism, argue Kingman and Vadera, citing statistics from the government’s own Industrial Strategy Advisory Council. Firms under five years old made 18% of all business sales in 2005; by 2021, the figure was only 10%. That decline is huge.

Here’s the gist of the paper: “It appears that ministers of both parties have become noticeably less interested in competition and disruption as a source of growth, and noticeably less supportive of robust, independent competition policy. They have also tended to look for the approbation of incumbent businesses and investors in their decision-making on policy.”

Note the “both parties” reference. The authors are not making a party political point. Significant pro-growth, pro-competition interventions have happened under both Tories and Labour. Big bang in the City was under Margaret Thatcher. The indefensible BAA airports monopoly in London, which saw Heathrow, Gatwick and Stansted owned by a single firm, was broken up in 2009 when Brown was at the helm. The fintech revolution was born from getting tougher on banks after the 2008 crash. It has only been more recently that governments “have come to see active pro-competition policy as a threat to growth, rather than a driver of it”, as the paper put it.

To be fair to the CMA, it would be hard to say it has gone wobbly under pressure. Doug Gurr, Bokkerink’s replacement, was regarded in some quarters as big tech’s patsy because he came from Amazon. In practice, the CMA has been lively with its “strategic market status” designations that can impose “conduct requirements” on tech firms. Google has been designated in search and search advertising ; Apple in mobile phones; and Microsoft may be added in business software.

All the same, political signals are important. They flag whether the government believes active competition policy boosts growth. In the age of AI, that is more important than ever. We don’t want AI giants to entrench an oligopoly before anybody notices, which is roughly what happened in the last tech revolution.

Encouragingly, the “public control” speech this week by Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, included a mini-reference to competition policy. “Where competition exists, it should be left to thrive,” she said, supported by a “strong, independent” CMA.

Was that a change of tone? Hard to say because ministers, even when they are sending mixed messages, always remember to mention the independence of the CMA. To clear things up, Haigh and Andy Burnham could adopt a few of Kingman and Vadera’s recommendations.

For example: say out loud that you want more competition and more disruption in the economy. Publish a scorecard of dynamism. Abolish the political “steer” to the CMA, which is a source of half the confusion. Reassert the primacy of its competition mandate. Give the body’s chair and chief executive single eight-year terms, as the governor of the Bank of England gets.

None feels incompatible with the “public control” stuff. All would send a clearer message about boosting growth and competition than we’re used to hearing.

title: Is this cycling’s ‘Moneyball’ moment? Inside the arms race for UCI points
author: James Witts
text:
"After my presentation in Barcelona, teams wanted to chat and compare their models with mine. This is a growing field, whether it's in search of points or simply improving performance as a whole." That's Louis Van Gaelen. The Belgian's undertaking a PhD in health and artificial intelligence at the University of Antwerp. As a side project, the keen cyclist dug deep into professional cycling and, as his presentation at this year's Science & Cycling Conference revealed, 'roster optimisation for maximal UCI points'. It's not the sexiest of titles, but Van Gaelen's hobby, aligned with the work of an increasing number of data scientists around the sport, is proving critical for not only a team's success but their survival. It's time to talk about the merits of not aiming for victory…

How does the system work?

The current UCI promotion and relegation system , rolled out in 2020, works in three-year cycles with 18 licences available to the men's WorldTour. The Women's WorldTour has 15 licences; however, demand for these spots is less competitive due to the limited number of teams willing to make the step up.

The 2026 season was the first season in the latest cycle, meaning points earned up to the end of 2028 will determine the WorldTour line-up for 2029 to 2031.

"All points from UCI-sanctioned races count towards the team total, but only the points accrued from the top-20 scoring riders," Van Gaelen adds. "Remaining at WorldTour can make or break a team."

That's because WorldTour status guarantees teams entry into cycling's biggest races, including the Tour de France, Giro d'Italia and Vuelta a España. Relegation means losing automatic invitations, reducing television exposure, sponsor value and commercial income. It also makes attracting top riders harder, potentially creating a vicious circle of declining competitiveness.

The UCI also assesses a team's non-sporting side, including the financial stability of the team, which is why they granted Team Picnic PostNL a truncated 12-month licence for 2026 . At the time of the ruling, the Dutch team hadn't finalised medium- to long-term backing with one of its sponsors, leaving the required fiscal guarantees for 2027 and 2028 incomplete. The Picnic turbulence continues to this day, heightened by serious allegations about team culture, with December 8, 2026 a key date in the calendar, as that's when the UCI is expected to confirm 2027 registrations.

But let's return to sporting criteria, as that's why the likes of Van Gaelen are in demand. His work looked to answer which riders a team should sign; which races each rider should participate in; and how a team can maximise its total UCI points across a season. The search involved combining two technologies: machine learning and mathematical optimisation.

Machine learning utilised 10 seasons' worth of data, covering thousands of riders and their previous performances, in addition to race profiles and course difficulty. "Inputting the course profiles was a laborious job," Van Gaelen says. "It involved uploading many, many course GPX files from an internet forum." Van Gaelen's machine-learning model then predicted the likely finishing order of riders in individual races, which were translated into expected UCI points using the relevant race's points scale.

The second part, mathematical optimisation, aimed to build the perfect roster by, for instance, matching climbers and sprinters to races where they're likeliest to score, by reducing clashes between teammates and setting a race-day ceiling at 85 days.

"With our optimised roster and focusing on one team in particular, we increased the points per rider from an average of 375.3 to 824.7," Van Gaelen explains. "Of course, there are limitations – our model didn't take into account fatigue, for example – but it's a promising proof of concept."

If Van Gaelen's work is good on paper, XDS Astana's is good in practice . The Kazakh team are the poster boys for optimising rosters in search of UCI points. At the end of the 2024 season, they were facing almost certain relegation, languishing 21st in the annual UCI rankings. But that's when they made one of their most important signings of recent times: data scientist Morgan Saussine.

One of the key implementations from Saussine's work was to prioritise top-10 finishes over individual victories. While historically teams would often organise their racing around one protected leader, with teammates sacrificing their own results to help that rider win, Saussine, who was unavailable for interview at the time of writing, identified there was much lower-hanging fruit to pick from in search of points.

Astana set about assembling a squad capable of scoring across different race categories, terrains and stages of the season. Into the squad came 14 new faces, including experienced riders such as Wout Poels, Diego Ulissi, Fausto Masnada and Mike Teunissen. The arrival of Chinese sponsor XDS provided additional financial resources to support the change. It worked, as they shot up the rankings to finish fourth in 2025 and so preserve their WorldTour status. Cofidis went down.

"Given the situation XDS Astana faced at the beginning of the 2025 season, when the team urgently needed UCI points, it's easy to see why a rider like Christian Scaroni was so invaluable," says researcher Simon Lucat. "Here's a rider who regularly finishes in the top-10 across a demanding race calendar."

Scaroni's importance to the cause was also highlighted this season with the 29-year-old Italian finishing inside the top-10 of one-day races or stages 33 times. He also won the overall at the Tour of Oman.

Lucat, a lifelong cycling fan and an economics student at Bocconi University in Milan, Italy, researched the inherent paradox that is professional cycling: results are attributed to individual riders, but they're collectively produced by a team.

"One of the main findings of my research is that the combined quality of the riders surrounding the leader can be just as important as the quality of the leader himself when it comes to accumulating UCI points," he says. "Strong teammates are valuable not only because they can help the leader achieve a better result, but also because they can score points themselves."

"The balance may also depend on the type of race," he adds. "Paris-Roubaix, for example, stood out in my analysis as a race where squad depth appeared to be particularly important. This makes sense if you think about the nature of the race, where a puncture or a crash can completely change a team's plans. Having several competitive riders gives you more options."

The original points detective

The likes of Van Gaelen and Lucat are building on the foundations laid by Raul Banqueri. In 2020, the diligent Spaniard waded through the UCI's 400-page road-racing regulations PDF in search of content for his Twitter account. It was needle-in-a-haystack stuff, but he pricked his fingers when he unearthed what many had missed. "I saw the UCI had started using sporting criteria to award licences and distribute wildcards to the WorldTour calendar," he says, "but almost nobody was reporting on it." He did, piquing the public's interest. And that of the professionals.

"When I started publishing my analyses of the points system, a multitude of WorldTour sports directors, performance directors and cyclists started following me on Twitter," he says. "Then in 2023 I started working with the Human Powered Health women's team . That season their licence was at risk, so I prepared a dashboard with advanced statistics on results and UCI points. We thoroughly analysed the calendar to identify which races they could score the most points in with the roster they had. The team focused more on flat races and minor races, tripled their UCI points compared to 2022 (from 914 to 3354) and managed to save their WorldTour licence.

"Nowadays, UCI points are no longer as important in women's cycling, as there aren't enough teams applying for the licence, but the dashboard remains valuable for the scouting process, signings and monitoring team performance."

That year, he also collaborated on projects with Visma-Lease a Bike, assisting the team's head of strategy, Patrick Broe, while in 2025 he saddled up with the Movistar Team women's squad, helping with data and video analysis. In short, Banqueri is hot property when it comes to delivering peak points and peak performance. So, what's his assessment of sniffing out peak points performers?

"Sprinters capable of getting over hills or specialists in hilly races with high top speed are increasingly sought after to claim points," he answers. "That includes Benoît Cosnefroy, Thomas Silva, Alex Aranburu, Natnael Tesfatsion and Lukáš Kubiš, who've all scored good points for their respective teams."

"In general, one-day races are significantly more profitable than stage races," he adds. "One-day races award the same points as the general classification of a race in the same category, and stages award very few points, except in the Grand Tours. Right now, I believe that ProSeries one-day races (250 points for the winner) are the most profitable in terms of UCI points."

Banqueri says an interesting development is the strategy and recruitment adopted by ProTeams, whose goal is the top 30 of the annual ranking in search of an invite to the Grand Tours. "These teams are the ones looking the most for races outside of Europe, especially in Asia, where the level is lower, since they can score a high percentage of their total seasonal UCI points. For WorldTeams, it's less profitable to travel to race in Asia, as it causes huge fatigue for their cyclists, and the UCI points they earn don't have as much impact on their total sum of UCI points.

"Also, some of the lower-level ProTeams, like Burgos BH, have signed cyclists from more immature cycling nations to take advantage of the UCI points they can win in National Championships and Continental Championships. All Continental Championships award the same points, as do National Championships, provided the nation participated in the previous World Championships. So, being the champion of Mauritius scores the same points as being the champion of France." To that end, five of Burgos BH's eight 2025 wins came at the national championships of Mauritius, plus Uruguay, Guatemala, Mongolia and Greece. In 2026, it was three from nine wins."

In both seasons, the Spanish outfit finished comfortably in the top-30, essentially guaranteeing them a wildcard spot at the Vuelta a España. These wildcard spots are keenly fought over for the same reasons that teams strain to cling onto WorldTour status, namely media exposure and sponsor value.

Downside of chasing points

For ProTeams, this short-term points grab could have long-term consequences for the sport. "This year, Bardiani had the lowest average age (only 22.4 years, according to Pro Cycling Stats) and ultimately fell out of the top 30 in the ranking, meaning they won't be invited to the Giro d'Italia in 2027," says Banqueri. "It's a bit unfair because a team like Bardiani is essential for developing young cyclists. It means in the future they'll probably have to sign more experienced cyclists to ensure results."

If there is a future. Come the end of the 2026 season, veteran team boss Bruno Reverberi couldn't contain his anger at the points system, calling the UCI "incompetent". Reverberi told the TriCiclo podcast that with no guarantees of invitation to the world's biggest races – they'd raced every Giro d'Italia since 1982 – they could soon be out of business. "How can you spend €5 million and not have the right to race? There is no future, and cycling has no future. We've already thought about closing in two years. In fact, we have taken four or five new riders and made them sign for only one year."…

title: Ford unveils the GT41 as it hopes to win Le Mans again
author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
text:
Sixty years ago, after two failed attempts, Ford won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with its GT40 race car. In the years since, the Blue Oval has been back to France more than a few times, with varying success. It could never replicate the GT40’s success winning overall, but it celebrated the 40th anniversary with a class win . Now it wants another shot at the really big trophy , and it debuted the car during the Detroit Lions-Chicago Bears football game today: meet the GT41.

“Revealing the Ford GT41 is a significant moment for everyone involved in this program,” said Dan Sayers, manager of Ford Racing’s Hypercar program. “It's the result of an enormous amount of work across our engineering, design, and development teams and an important milestone on our journey towards 2027. We know the scale of the challenge ahead—the level of competition in Hypercar is incredibly high, and there are no shortcuts to success. Our focus has been on building the right foundations, bringing together the right people and making sure we learn as much as possible from every stage of development.”

The video was directed by Zack Snyder and features Matt Damon’s voice-over.

Like many other entrants in the World Endurance Championship’s Hypercar class, Ford has chosen the rear-wheel-drive LMDh technical approach rather than building the GT41 entirely from scratch, as Ferrari and Aston Martin do with their cars. LMDh cars start with one of four approved carbon fiber chassis—in this case, Ford is working with Oreca, which has also partnered with Genesis and Acura.

title: Poundland staff fear they’ll be left out in the cold for Christmas. When will workers have a say in their future? | Polly Toynbee
author: Polly Toynbee
text:
High streets and ultimately the taxpayer will suffer from the chain’s liquidation. Who will benefit? The company that snapped up this institution for just £1

W hen the bad news came through on his mobile on Wednesday afternoon, the manager of Poundland’s store in Camden, north London, Aboud, summoned all his staff. “One lad, been here 11 years, was in tears and ran out of the store, he was so upset. This is home and family for many of them.”

They are among 11,000 staff whose jobs are now at risk, but some shops might get bought by other chains. “Do you know,” Aboud asks me, “can we find out if this store might be saved?” I can’t, and the liquidators are only just starting work. He can no longer get through to his senior regional manager: “He doesn’t pick up now.”

He was told that day to keep the shop looking neat (“As I always do”), but more shelves are bare, the Christmas glitz a mockery to those fearing they’ll have no job by then. Now he is worrying about pay. “They paid us early this week and I don’t know why. Does it mean that’s it, no more?” Will stock deliveries stop? On Thursday, a conference call reassures them wages will be paid and he tells his staff to hang in there – to “have faith” that this store survives.

In this largest retail bust for a decade, 600 high streets stand to lose an anchor store. Many will join the boarded-up shopfronts that destroy a sense of thriving community. How did it come to this?

In 2025 Gordon Brothers, a company that specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, bought Poundland for £1. As part of the terms for taking over the company, it inherited a shareholder loan, and as such was owed £22.5m. Gordon Brothers rejected various offers to buy the business because of concerns the deals would not pay off that loan. Despite Poundland management taking the store into profit last year, the parent company argued that it was “still vulnerable” to inflation and any downturn in profits. However, Gordon Brothers restricted access to funds for day-to-day operations, meaning that stock was not being replenished, affecting sales.

Gordon Brothers said after the news broke this week : “First and foremost, our thoughts are with Poundland colleagues. We recognise how difficult the continued uncertainty is for them.” But Poundland staff feel their concerns are being placed neither “first” nor “foremost”. Poundland’s founder, Steve Smith, who started with one shop in Burton-on-Trent 36 years ago, warns that of the 2,000 suppliers due to be affected, most only supply to Poundland , so he expects more collapses and job losses, leaving a long trail of disaster. Critics have said Gordon Brothers stands to make its loans back and more from any insolvency process, however.

Andy Burnham’s Makerfield constituency has a large Poundland distribution centre. “Poundland is part of the fabric of high streets and communities up and down the country,” the prime minister said, with Downing Street promising to do all it can. But that’s hardly reassuring when the voices of government were ignored during the process of trying to save the company. Liam Byrne, chair of the business select committee, has summoned Mark Newton-Jones, the European director of Gordon Brothers, to a public hearing, keen to find out why it turned down offers, including one from Martin Property Group, owners of National Car Parks. Byrne gives me some estimates relating to where the money has gone. “They already made £18.3m in fees and charges. They will get the return of their £22m loan. They have starved Poundland into administration by denying access to its £63m bank account to restock and trade” – though Gordon Brothers denies it. Byrne adds: “This is not only terrible for the workers but for taxpayers too, as the state picks up any potential unpaid redundancy entitlement or tax.”

Lessons must be learned, he tells me. “Do we want ‘greed is good’ market supremacy?” It’s a “morality tale” that demands reform of company law, he says. He would change Section 172 of the Companies Act that gives primacy to shareholders. These laws enable private equity and restructuring firms to overload businesses with debt, as well as extract “proxy dividends” through debt repayments, and break up companies at the expense of high-street jobs. It’s time, he says, to put employees on company boards, German-style.

Despite firms lobbying about “over-regulation” of business, time and again we get a jolting reminder of where the power lies. Here’s a small but telling anecdote. Last week the business committee was due for a long-arranged visit to an Amazon “fulfilment centre”, letting the company display its working conditions. But the committee pulled out at the last minute when Amazon refused to let it speak to GMB union reps there , who might have had a different story to tell. This came just weeks after the union had applied for access rights to allow its reps to recruit inside the Coventry warehouse, under new powers within the Employment Rights Act. This may be an augury of friction to come. Coventry is where the GMB campaigned hard at Amazon for 12 years for union recognition , but lost a vote after the company subjected staff to six-hour union-bashing seminars and flooded the place with obedient new workers, amid threats of delayed wage rises.

Labour’s attempt to restore and rebalance the muscle of workforces against the steel of capital faces a drumbeat of business lobby objections to new employment rights that both the Tories and Reform UK have pledged to abolish. Put that into the context of how weak workers’ rights have become since Margaret Thatcher’s 1980s assaults. Union membership fell from 13m in 1979 to 6.5m by 2024 . Loss of influence led to a sharp fall in pay as a proportion of GDP , from 72% in 1975 (the most equal year in history) to 59% last year.…

title: Neuville, Fourmaux and Meeke in latest Rally2 test for Hyundai
Ferrari facing 'very challenging times' - Hamilton
text:
Lewis Hamilton says Ferrari are facing "very, very challenging times" as a result of the series of on-track incidents between himself and team-mate Charles Leclerc.

The two drivers had talks on Thursday after arriving at the Qatar Grand Prix to discuss the fall-out from their collision in the race in Las Vegas last weekend, which team boss Frederic Vasseur said was "completely unacceptable" .

Both said the conclusion of those discussions would "stay internal" but admitted a solution needed to be found.

Hamilton said: "I like to think that we're stronger from these difficult...

"If everything was just great all the time, I don't think you learn anything when you're winning all the time. You learn really through the hardest times.

"These are definitely very, very challenging times for Fred and Charles and I."

Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A

Hamilton-Leclerc collision 'completely unacceptable'

Leclerc admitted that "at the moment it's not working" and said there was "tension around that we need to dissipate".

The incident in Las Vegas was the second in three races between Hamilton and Leclerc .

In Mexico City last month, their battle on the first lap led to them handing victory to Red Bull's Max Verstappen in a race that Ferrari should have finished one-two.

After that event. Hamilton said Ferrari "had to have some serious talks behind closed doors" and that the team had "big, big problems".

They had those talks in the next race in Brazil, brokered by Vasseur, only for there to be two flashpoints in Las Vegas.

Hamilton was first penalised 10 seconds for gaining an advantage by cutting the track while racing with McLaren's Lando Norris, in an incident to which Leclerc was also in close proximity.

And then Leclerc received a 10-second penalty for pitching Hamilton into a spin.

Leclerc said: "We have a very good relationship outside the car with Lewis.

"I wouldn't say the atmosphere was good because we are disappointed by the situation we are in.

"But we are all grown up and responsible and we have to find a solution and there is also a big willingness to find a solution."

Leclerc said the incidents kept happening because "we are two very strong drivers who want to finish one ahead of the other".

He added: "I do believe some level of tension is always there in top teams when you have two drivers.

"If you look this year there have been more than 10 times we have started side by side. We are always together. So a certain amount of tension is obviously always there, but it doesn't necessarily have to escalate and that is why we need to find a solution and fix that."

Hamilton added: "I have no doubts that next year we'll come back working hard together and in a better place. I think we'll quickly get better processes in place so that we can really get a right team."

title: When will Poundland shops close? Five key questions answered
text:
Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas.

The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the company.

This is the question that is most difficult to answer.

Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it.

Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome.

When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.

Before the collapse, Fortress, which owns rival budget chain Poundstretcher, was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand.

But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. The BBC understands it is considering selling Poundstretcher, a move first reported by Bloomberg.

A decision on Poundstretcher could come before the end of this week. However, Fortress has declined to comment.

When the chain was sold by Pepco last year for £1 it was struggling. It suffered a £68m loss that year.

Poundland's managing director Barry Williams said Poundland had been seeing a "strong recovery" and recorded a profit by one measure in the first nine months of this year.

Poundland's management paint a picture of a retailer that was turning a corner until the owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, pulled the plug on funding for day-to-day expenses such as buying stock.

The Usdaw union, which represents shopworkers, claim the owners forced Poundland into administration.

Labour MP Antonia Bance said she was "pretty appalled" by the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the past few weeks, and that it was going to make much bigger profits by breaking up the business rather than by keeping it going.

However, Gordon Brothers insisted the business was only turning a profit on paper, and had missed budget forecasts.

A spokeswoman said while the management team had made £100m in cost reductions, the business had moved from a £70m loss to "around break-even".

"Break-even is different from generating the cash needed to buy stock, invest, and withstand increasing economic pressures," the spokeswoman said. "A few good weeks do not make a turnaround."

Poundland repeatedly missed budget targets over the year, the spokeswoman added.

Gordon Brothers was concerned that as inflation goes up next year, those pressures would have helped to make the business unviable, it said.

And Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency agency Begbies Traynor, said Poundland's collapse "seemed somehow inevitable" due to challenges facing retailers - including higher costs to employ staff.

Stores are still trading while the administrators work out if the business is viable.

The funds locked up by Gordon Brothers - at the last count about £70m - have now been released by the administrators.

This has turned the taps back on, so staff will continue to be paid in the run-up to Christmas, and so will suppliers.

But here's the catch: the administrators have a legal obligation to maximise value for "secured" creditors. It means the owners, Gordon Brothers, are at the head of the queue for being paid back the loans that were stumbling blocks in the negotiations.

But more importantly for staff, if the administrators can get more value by breaking up the business than by selling it as a whole, then that is what they have to do, even if the business would be viable.

If the business is broken up and its stores are sold off, the new owners would not be obliged to keep staff on.

From 26 November you will not get a refund for goods if you change your mind about the purchase. If the item is faulty you will still get a refund.

The immediate reason Poundland collapsed was that Gordon Brothers locked up funds for the day-to-day running of the business, including to pay suppliers.

This meant that stock was running low at Poundland.

But those funds have now been unlocked, meaning suppliers can be paid, and supply chains can be re-established, at least in the short term.

If an item is on the shelves, then shoppers can buy it.

Administrators will have to get the best value for creditors, which could mean selling the business as it stands.

But if Poundland is broken up, administrators could sell the brand without the stores, or the brand along with some of the stores, or the stores without the Poundland brand, to other retailers.

As a result there could be fewer discount stores on the High Street, providing less incentive for other retailers to keep prices down.

"Poundland is a place they go on the High Street to get bargains and... given the cost of living challenges we face, that is of concern to us in government," Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, told the BBC on Thursday.

Poundland's customers may well turn to rival budget retailers in the hunt for bargains.

Sven Nys' cyclo-cross team has swiftly found a new title sponsor following the withdrawal of Glowi , owner of named sponsor Het Poetsbureau.

The team, which is led by women's world champion Lucinda Brand and men's European champion Thibau Nys , welcomes electrical retailer Elektro Loeters as a new title sponsor alongside Baloise Verzekeringen.

The new sponsorship will begin on January 1, 2027, though the length of the deal hasn't been announced.

"Elektro Loeters embodies the same winning mentality that we strive for every day," team manager Sven Nys said in an Instagram post announcing the news.

The deal came about quickly, the team confirmed, with Elektro Loeters only approaching them in recent weeks.

"When you see an opportunity, you have to act quickly. We immediately felt a connection with the team’s vision and ambitions. Five days later, an agreement was already on the table. It shows just how similar entrepreneurship and top-level sport are."

The team, currently known as Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions, have been the most successful during the 2026-27 cyclo-cross season so far with 12 victories.

Nys has four wins, including three rounds of the X2O Trofee, while Brand has six, including two apiece in the X2O Trofee and Superprestige. Both triumphed at the UEC Cyclo-cross European Championships in Zeddam earlier this month.

Like the team, Elektro Loeters is also experiencing success, with the company planning to open five new stores in Flanders in addition to its 10 pre-existing stores.

"Elektro Loeters embodies the same winning mentality that we strive for every day. Their growth story, entrepreneurial spirit and drive are a perfect match for our values. We are therefore looking forward to further developing this partnership over the coming months and putting it into action together," said Sven Nys.

Brand and Thibau Nys will lead the team in their new identity alongside other key riders Pim Ronhaar and Annemarie Worst. However, this will be Brand's penultimate cyclo-cross season, as the Dutchwoman will retire from racing in April 2028.

You Can Now Buy a 28-Gram, CNC-Machined Titanium Dynamo Taillight—If You’re One of 30 Buyers
author: Josh Ross
text:
Berlin-based component brand Allygn has released a limited-edition titanium version of its EdelMü dynamo taillight, swapping the standard model’s aluminum housing for CNC-machined titanium for an extremely limited initial run.

The point of this kind of titanium extravagance is obviously to look great, but it does also solve a problem. For riders building custom randonneuring, bikepacking or commuter bikes, dynamo lighting has always been an aesthetic mismatch. While SON’s Edelux headlights are a staple on handmade builds, rear dynamo lights tend to look like an afterthought. Allygn founder and Fern Bicycles framebuilder Flo Haeussler originally designed the EdelMü to close that gap, taking the proven German-made internals from a Busch & Müller Mü taillight and housing them in a small, machined barrel that echoes the look of the Edelux.

It’s a natural problem for Haeussler to solve, as it’s the stated driving force behind the brand. Allygn Components specifically aims “for a fully integrated bicycle design, where every part blends seamlessly into each bike’s overall concept, both functionally and aesthetically.”

Which is why, as good as the EdelMü is, the new titanium version goes even further. The design keeps that exact formula but upgrades the outer shell from 6061 aluminum to high-polished, CNC-machined titanium.

Inside, nothing changes from a functional standpoint. The light ships with standard 6V AC dynamo internals from Busch & Müller, complete with capacitors to keep the stand light illuminated when stopped at intersections. Allygn says the housing can also accommodate 5-15V DC Mü internals for riders running e-bike or battery setups. Small cutouts machined into the titanium body provide side visibility.

The light measures 30.2 mm long with a 20.6 mm diameter at the plastic holder, and Allygn lists the weight at 28 grams including the uncut wiring and M3 bolt. Hardware consists of black zinc-nickel-plated stainless steel M4 and M5 bolts.

Two mounting configurations are available: an M6 direct braze-on option for custom frames and a POM ring mount. The ring-mount version is designed to pair with the rear light mount from fellow Berlin outfit Drust Cycles. Framebuilders can also source braze-ons directly from Allygn.

The titanium EdelMü taillight retails for €150, or roughly $142 for U.S. buyers through Fern Bicycles after German VAT is deducted at checkout (before any applicable import duties). A bundle pairing the ring-mount light with a matching titanium Drust Cycles mount is also available for €185.

Because only 30 lights are included in this first batch, availability is tight. Riders and builders can order through the Fern Bicycles website or contact Allygn directly for more information.

title: Politician hosts 400,000 guests at daughter’s wedding in India’s poorest state
author: Amrit Dhillon in Delhi
text:
Six helipads built and feast prepared by 500 cooks for wedding hosted by Anant Singh, an MP charged with murder

It takes a brave soul to try to match the mythic opulence of the wedding arranged by the Indian billionaire Mukesh Ambani for his son Anant in 2024. Estimates of the cost for the months-long celebration ran to at least $600m, with world leaders and celebrities among those on the guest list.

Smaller fry though he is, Anant Singh, a legislator in India’s poorest state, Bihar, gave it his best shot on Wednesday, albeit in a rustic rural setting, for the nuptials of his daughter Shivangi Singh, and Rishikesh Kumar, an MBA student from Georgia State University in Atlanta.

About 400,000 guests were hosted across 2.5 hectares at the family home in the village of Nadawa – a staggering figure even by the standards of India’s famed extravagant weddings. Guests were treated to 500,000 pieces of traditional sweets, and a feast prepared by an army of 500 chefs and cooks, Singh’s confidant Munna Singh told Agence France-Presse. One thousand kgs of mutton were reportedly used for kebabs and curries. Six makeshift helipads were erected for VIPs flying in from across India.

Kumar arrived at the venue in sunglasses and waving an orange scarf in a convoy of 151 cars (Hindus consider uneven numbers to be lucky). Among the gifts for the groom was a Land Rover Defender.

The roads leading to the venue were so choked with cars before the wedding that one guest escaped the gridlock, The Times of India reported, by jumping on a tractor and driving across the surrounding fields.

Guests were also treated to elaborate flower arrangements featuring blooms imported from China, and a fireworks display.

Instead of a DJ for entertainment, Singh planned a horse race. Gatecrashers clambered up into trees and on to electricity towers to catch a glimpse of the race, but the chaos and tumult was so great it had to be cancelled at the 11th hour. Lying around somewhere amid the wedding detritus was the SUV that would have gone to the winner.

Singh is a controversial figure. Elected five times to the state assembly, he has 28 criminal cases pending against him ranging from murder and attempted murder to extortion and kidnapping. All the cases are listed on the website of the Association for Democratic Reforms, an NGO trying to improve governance and strengthen democracy. Singh denies any wrongdoing.

In a television interview before the wedding, he pooh poohed the idea that there was anything unusual about the scale of the wedding preparations. “I laid on exactly the same thing for my elder daughter,” he said.

India’s wedding season has just kicked off. Between now and 15 December, an estimated 5.2m weddings are expected to take place across the country.

title: New UK-EU treaty has 10-year termination clause
text:
The government and the EU are set to publish the texts of two treaties that were agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.

The treaties will be published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation which is designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The BBC understands the deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.

Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal and Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.

The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the long-term UK-EU relationship.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.

New assessments of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country are also expected.

EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme

Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students

Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."

The BBC understands that a plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text will also contain finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, will also be detailed in the legislation.

Such powers could enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week , the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".
