title: Faulty electrical goods returned to UK supermarkets ending up on Ghana ‘megadump’
author: Sandra Laville Environment correspondent
text:
Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as masks, investigation alleges

Electrical goods that were returned as faulty to leading British stores including Tesco , Argos and Asda have been found dumped on a waste tip in Ghana, an investigation has found.

The faulty electrical appliances, including toasters and slow cookers, had been returned to major UK supermarkets. They were found at Agbogbloshie, one of the world’s largest e-waste sites, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, a joint investigation by Unearthed and Greenpeace Africa has found. The findings raise serious questions about e-waste export rules.

Mountains of household items are burned and stripped down at the tip by workers without protection such as gloves and masks, the investigation alleges.

Exporting broken electrical goods to Africa is illegal under UK waste export rules in almost every circumstance.

Tesco own brand slow cookers, toasters and Crockpot branded slow cookers, including at least one with a Tesco label, were found on the Accra dump.

Tesco said on Thursday it had suspended its third-party electronic waste management providers with immediate effect while it completed a full audit of them and their practices.

“We’re extremely concerned about these claims … We remain committed to removing or reducing the waste across our operations wherever we can and we work closely with experts to ensure we handle materials responsibly, in line with legal requirements and our own robust standards,” the store said.

Argos items including its own brand Cookworks products, slow cookers, toasters and food slicers were found at the dump.

Argos also said it was mounting an investigation into how the items had ended up there.

“As a responsible retailer, we have processes in place for products returned to Argos. We take these findings seriously and are reviewing the information provided to establish what further action is needed to ensure our requirements are met,” Argos said in a statement.

The investigation found dozens more British items bearing returns labels for sale, including many marked as faulty, being sold in secondhand shops in the area.

Shopkeepers said they had bought the items from brokers in the UK, who provided them as mixed shipments of home electrical equipment.

“The percentage of unusable products varies [by shipment] but sometimes it can be about 10%,” one vendor said. “What do I do with the broken ones? I put them in this box and the Agbogbloshie boys come to collect it.”

All major UK retailers who sell electrical goods operate a take-back scheme which requires them to accept and recycle disused items – for example, a shopper who brings in their old toaster when they buy a new one. The goods should be logged as e-waste and contribute to stores meeting their government-mandated recycling targets.

Under the waste electrical and electronic equipment (WEEE) regulations, the goods should be passed on to approved processors. They can only be exported if the shipper can prove they will be handled in high-quality facilities.

No facilities in west Africa are approved to receive British WEEE, according to the Environment Agency .

“Ghana is not a dumping ground for broken appliances or failed retail returns from the UK,” Joshua Awuku-Apaw, a Ghanaian environmental consultant, told Unearthed. “Shipping faulty, non-functional kitchen appliances abroad under the cover of ‘reuse’ or ‘second-hand trade’ shifts the financial, environmental, and health costs of overconsumption on to Ghanaian communities and workers … Ghana’s communities should not bear the health burden of UK retail waste.”

The investigation traced the route by which the products could have ended up in Ghana. When recently bought items are returned to shops for a refund, even when they are being returned because they are faulty, they can enter a separate stream, the liquidation market, along with other consumer returns, the investigation found.

“Just because somebody in the supermarket says it’s not working, doesn’t always mean they’ve technically declared it as waste,” said e-waste expert Mark Sayers.

Many of the items Greenpeace found in Agbogbloshie and second-hand stores had stickers labelling the goods as “untested return”.

The investigation alleged that returned goods are often sold off in bulk, at a fraction of their shop shelf-price. Sometimes this takes place via the retailers’ own stock liquidation channels where pallets of returns, including job lots of small household electricals, are sold.

The lots are bought by “jobbers” – individuals and small businesses who buy the goods by the palletload and set about extracting any value they can – whether by listing items individually on eBay or Vinted, selling them in bargain-bin stores or exporting them.

Jim Puckett, founder of Basel Action Network, which campaigns against the export of e-waste to poorer countries, said that treating untested returns as anything other than waste was a “major loophole”.

“It should be considered waste until proven otherwise,” he said. “Especially if people are buying it at auction or whatever and shipping it all around the world.”

An Environment Agency spokesperson said: “Illegal waste exports are a serious crime. There is no excuse for exporting waste to be dumped or landfilled overseas. Waste leaving England must be sent for legitimate recovery or recycling.

“New controls mean exports of waste electrical and electronic equipment must be notified and approved before they leave the country. The Environment Agency is using intelligence to intervene earlier, target suspicious shipments and disrupt the criminals behind illegal waste exports.”

“Anyone who breaks the law risks having shipments stopped, facing prosecution and financial penalties. Waste criminals should be in no doubt, we are watching, we are acting and you will face the consequences.”…

title: Manchester United, Liverpool and Spurs using same law firm to set up legal claim against City
author: Exclusive by Matt Hughes
text:
Rivals engage law firm Wiggin as they seek damages

Claim could be worth hundreds of millions of pounds

Manchester United, Liverpool and Tottenham are using the same law firm to prepare a legal claim against Manchester City for breaking the Premier League’s financial rules that could be worth hundreds of millions of pounds.

The clubs have engaged the services of the London-based media, entertainment and technology specialists Wiggin. Arsenal are using their retained lawyers, HFS Kramer, to prepare their own claim.

A source with knowledge of the case disclosed there had been a degree of cooperation between the clubs using Wiggin, because they have also engaged the same analysts to assess the size of the potential losses allegedly caused by City’s financial cheating , but that they would bring separate claims for damages.

“The cases are similar but different,” the source said. “The ultimate causation may be the same, but the damages will be different so they will be separate claims.”

Another source disclosed that Tottenham initially engaged Wiggin while Daniel Levy was the chair and were the first club to make legal moves against City after they were charged with financial fair play breaches in February 2023, with United and Liverpool following their lead.

Those three clubs and Arsenal lodged legal notices in November 2024 reserving their right to seek compensation against City to avoid their potential claims being ruled time-barred, one of the mechanisms through which City succeeded in 2020 in having a two-year ban from the Champions League imposed by Uefa for similar alleged offences lifted by the court of arbitration for sport.

Standard breach of contract claims have a six-year statute limitation from the moment they are made public, and with the allegations of City’s rule-breaking first published in the German news magazine Der Spiegel in November 2018, four of the other members of the big six acted to reserve their rights.

Chelsea did not instruct lawyers to begin a claim against City at that point, and are not believed to have done so since, despite the fact that extensions to the time limit can be granted in cases of fraud and concealment.

The four clubs who are preparing legal action have stepped up their activities since the Premier League announced in September that City had been found guilty of the vast majority of more than 100 charges against them, with an independent commission ruling that the club had artificially inflated its income by more than £900m through the use of “sham contracts” between 2009 and 2018.

Tottenham are likely to make the biggest claim against City because they missed out on Champions League qualification to them on four occasions during that period, with dropping into the Europa League costing them more than £120m.

United and Liverpool finished second in the Premier League to City during years when City have been found to have inflated their income, in 2012 and 2014 respectively, costing them prize money and commercial revenue and bonuses.

Arsenal missed out on Champions League qualification by finishing fifth in the Premier League in 2017, the start of a six-season run outside Europe’s elite competition that combined will have cost them hundreds of millions of pounds, as City ended up third.

Arsenal also sold five key players to City during the period of their breaches – Kolo Touré, Gaël Clichy, Emmanuel Adebayor, Bacary Sagna and Samir Nasri – and may claim additional losses on the grounds that their purchases were artificially funded.

Everton, Newcastle and Chelsea also missed out on Champions League places during the relevant period, and numerous clubs including Hull were relegated in part owing to their results against City.

Stoke lost the 2011 FA Cup final to City, costing them a Europa League place, and their then manager, Tony Pulis, said in October that the club should be awarded the trophy.

City have denied wrongdoing since being charged almost four years ago and have launched an appeal against the independent commission’s verdict , which will be heard by a new three-person panel next month. After launching their appeal in October, City issued a statement saying the commission’s judgment contained “multiple clear material errors of law, principle and fact and is unsafe” and that “the club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all its positions, relating to this case”.

title: China reserves right to take ‘necessary measures’ after Trump’s new tariff proposals
author: Rebecca Bailey and agencies
text:
Brazil indignant about proposed tariffs on sugar and aircraft, while Beijing says new levies amount to ‘political manipulation’

Trump proposing new tariffs on 14 partners including China and EU

Brazil has said it will not bend to the new US tariff “threat” and China accused Washington of “political manipulation” in the wake of Donald Trump’s latest economic salvo against 14 major trading partners.

Brazil’s government said on Wednesday: “Brazil will not yield to this type of threat”, adding in its statement that the “unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the framework of the ongoing bilateral negotiating process”.

It voiced particular indignation at US proposals for higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a change that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

It added that Brazil would continue to negotiate “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products”.

Brazil was singled out in the announcement after trade talks stalled. The Trump administration claimed on Wednesday that the new tariffs would be consistent with trade deals that the US reached last year with dozens of countries.

The new tariffs are being imposed under a law which allowed the president to target countries the US had found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices. Jamieson Greer, the US trade representative, told CNBC that many US trading partners had adopted “market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America’s manufacturing base.”

The Trump administration’s new tariff rates would be capped at lower ​levels ‌agreed under ​trade deals ​that have already been concluded or remain under negotiation.

The administration will seek feedback from affected industries and hold a hearing on 25 January, suggesting the final duties won’t take effect until February or March.

China is potentially facing one of the biggest hits. The US said China would face the highest capped rate of 20%, which in some cases will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%. The US and China last year reached a trade truce but that is set to expire on 10 January 2027.

A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected allegations that China was ‌a source of ⁠excess capacity, but stopped short of threatening retaliation.

“The so-called issue of ‘industrial overcapacity’ does not really exist and should not be used as a pretext for political manipulation,” the spokesperson said, urging the two sides to jointly deliver on agreements secured between Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

Earlier, China’s foreign ministry restated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for $30bn worth of Chinese goods in line with the deal. “We’ve talked to our trading partners about this – they know what we’re proposing,” Greer said. “I think a lot of this is baked in.”

Some US analysts criticised the duties as too weak to change China’s trade practices.

China “is a bigger source of excess production than the rest of the world combined,” said Derek Scissors, senior fellow at the American Enterprise Institute. Yet Wednesday’s proposal “barely raises existing tariffs on China and will make no difference to the country’s trade behaviour.”

The EU said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the US to stick by a deal struck last year. “The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action,” European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said.

Vietnam’s trade ministry said it was ⁠working with the US to complete its trade deal as soon ⁠as possible and would coordinate with relevant US agencies.

It added it was “preparing ​and submitting ​rebuttal comments on the ​preliminary findings as well as on inaccurate submissions ​and allegations ‌made by ​interested ​parties.”

In response to the US announcement, the Indian government denied it had any structural excess capacity in ⁠any sector, ⁠adding that it remained committed to an early conclusion of ⁠a trade deal between the two countries. Greer has said the tariff ⁠on Indian imports would be capped at 17% if a trade deal was struck.

Taiwan was also singled out for new tariffs, but Taipei on Thursday said it was confident it would keep its existing ⁠15% tariff rate.

Taipei and Washington signed trade deals in January and February of ‌this year, which secured preferential treatment for semiconductors and other tech product which account for ​over 70% of Taiwan’s exports to the US.

Other countries and regions affected by the new tariffs include Bangladesh, ‌Cambodia, the European Union, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, and Thailand.

Tokyo’s top government spokesman, Minoru Kihara, said it was “regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced”.

And Singapore’s government said it was “very disappointed” with the proposals and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidising manufacturing.

Trump’s latest round of tariffs may be here to stay despite the Democrats’ electoral sweep in the US midterms. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.

However Democratic Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will take over the finance committee next year, said he would “use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariffs chaos.”…

title: The most dramatic moments of the 2026 cycling season – Shock retirements, nail-biting sprints and tense transfers
author: Matilda Price
text:
2026 is coming to an end, with training camps about to begin and attention already shifting to the 2027 racing season. Here at , we've already been reviewing many aspects of the season just gone, such as the best neo pros and best domestiques , but what about the moments that defined the year?

Rather than best moments – because who could ever choose just 10? – we've gone back through the headlines to identify the 10 most dramatic moments of the 2026 season, the stories that shocked all of us and the racing that got the excitement brewing.

From sudden retirements and high-profile crashes to tensions bubbling over at the biggest races on the calendar, as well as thrilling sprints and a debate about anti-doping, here are the 10 moments that we think delivered the drama in 2026.

Simon Yates' shock retirement

Rewind all the way to the start of the year, and things kicked off with a bang before the racing had even really started, with Simon Yates shocking the world with the news of his retirement . Rumours of Yates thinking about an early exit from the sport had been swirling, but after he'd won the Giro d'Italia, completed the 2025 season and started winter training and 2026 camps with Visma-Lease a Bike, it seemed like that must be off the table. Apparently not.

One day he was out training in Visma kit, and the next he announced his retirement just a few days into January. It was a surprise to not just the cycling world, but to his team too, who were then left scrambling and a rider short for the rest of the season. To bow out on such a high, as the Giro champion with a full and busy schedule, is practically unheard of and dominated the headlines for weeks as we collected reactions from around the peloton – mainly equally as surprised as we were.

Even to this day, Yates has not opened up all that much about why he made his decision when he did, instead just slipping back into normal life. Whilst it might not have felt that dramatic to him, it was certainly one of the defining moments of the first part of the 2026 season.

A frightening crash at Milan-San Remo Women

I wouldn't usually include a crash in a list like this, but if I am thinking of moments that were shocking and dramatic to their core, the scary crash involving Debora Silvestri, Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney and Kim Le Court-Pienaar at Milan-San Remo Women was one of them. Coming off the Cipressa at high speed, several riders came down hard, with Silvestri the worst off as she crashed over the guardrails and fell several feet onto concrete.

This isn't the kind of drama we want to celebrate or remember, but it was a frightening moment that raised questions about safety, speed and risk – questions that would continue through the season. Silvestri's myriad of injuries and long stay in hospital, including needing breathing support, was a stark reminder of just how much danger cyclists face with very, very little protection between them and hitting the tarmac and over 60kph.

The intense debate about safety hadn't quite kicked off back in March, but it became a defining conversation of the 2026 season, and this crash will go down as one of the types of incidents we must work harder to avoid, or at least offer riders more protection from.

The final sprint of men's Paris-Roubaix

The final sprint of Paris-Roubaix is always one of cycling's most electrifying moments, and this year was no different, with the velodrome finales of both the men's and women's races offering spectacular, hold-your-breath racing. Franziska Koch bettering both Marianne Vos and Pauline Ferrand-Prévot was an enormous underdog win moment in the women's race, but the one that will really, really stick with me is the climax of the men's race.

The whole race was packed to the brim with drama, to be truthful, but that was distilled into a few minutes of pure adrenaline as the leaders entered the Roubaix velodrome. Wout van Aert vs Tadej Pogačar. Knowing what we do about both riders it felt in a way like the story might already be written. Van Aert is the rider more likely to win Roubaix, given the reigning Tour de France champion is usually nowhere near the top of the list of favourites. But the mythology of these two riders made it different; Pogačar is the rider who wins at will, and Van Aert is the one who has been runner-up more times than you can count. I had a sinking feeling that the Belgian star was going to be denied yet again by the specialism-defying Slovenian.

That's why, when Van Aert drew slightly ahead of Pogačar in the sprint and soared to a fantastic win, it felt like a shock and a huge moment. It was somehow the obvious result and one that felt like it could easily slip through Van Aert's fingers, but it didn't.

Pogačar had been beaten – a very rare occurrence indeed – and Van Aert had scored his first cobbled Monument win in a wildly emotional moment. It was a gripping sprint to round out a hugely dramatic race, and is surely one of the most memorable moments of 2026.

Falling ice on the Colle delle Finestre

The penultimate stage of the women's Giro d'Italia should have been one of the most dramatic days of the women's calendar as they went up and over the Colle delle Finestre, but it ended up delivering the drama in different ways than we expected.

Instead of going up and over the mythical gravel climb and climbing back up to Sestriere for the finish, the stage was shortened mid-race due to the risk of falling ice of the top of the Finestre . This meant that the Giro's most epic stage was suddenly turned on its head, with riders having to adapt their tactics and plans on the road, leading to an all-out battle on the climb – which, ironically, might not have happened had the stage maintained its full length.

Four riders came towards the revised finish line together, with Demi Vollering powering away from Bella Holmgren, Antonia Niedermaier and Anna van der Breggen to pull closer to the overall lead, which she would go on to grab away from Van der Breggen on the final stage. All this unfolded in the ominous mist atop the Finestre, making for truly dramatic scenes.

Overnight testing debate at the Tour de France

The Tour de France hasn't faced actual doping drama for several years now, with a few unfruitful raids the most we've seen and a long way away from the mid-race positives and expulsions we were used to seeing a few years ago. But the 2026 edition still found a way to weave a controversial doping storyline into its plot.

The drama ended up not being about doping itself, but testing, when several top names including Pogačar and Vingegaard revealed that they had been woken in the middle of the night by testers . Gloss over the fact that riders aren't actually meant to reveal stuff like that – the anti-doping authority's element of surprise is a bit undermined if riders understand their tactics – and it was soon pretty much the biggest story of the middle of the race. Debate raged on over whether it was ethical to wake tired riders in the early hours as they tried to recover before another stage, and about whether this meant there was suspicion over the riders involved (to be clear, such tests do not imply any suspicion).

As far as we're aware, nothing came of those midnight tests, with the date for results to be returned long gone by now, but it certainly brought the topic of testing and doping back into the spotlight at the Tour, and stirred up the drama in a race that wasn't exactly full of that racing-wise.

Jonas Vingegaard crashes out of the Tour

The first of two really dramatic GC crashes over the summer, Jonas Vingegaard's Tour de France was over in the blink of an eye when he crashed heavily on a nondescript corner on stage 15. It was clear pretty quickly that he was not going to continue, as he clutched his arm in a way we all recognise as a surefire sign of a broken collarbone – an injury no one can race through. It was a shocking and sad sight, and heavily shaped the rest of the race.

Suddenly, the only rider who has ever challenged Tadej Pogačar at the Tour was out of the running, and even if he was already 4:30 down at that stage, any tiny hope of a miraculous turnaround was definitively gone. It felt like Pogačar's fifth win was confirmed in that moment.

As it turned out, that one crash would go on to have further reaching effects than we could have imagined at the time, with Vingegaard ultimately opting not to return to racing at all in 2026, and rumours even brewing that retirement was on his mind after another big crash in the sport he has already criticised for being too dangerous. Thankfully, he's since confirmed that he's not bowing out just yet, but that crash may still go down as a defining moment in his career.

A wild weekend in Nice to close out the Tour de France Femmes

If fans had felt that the Tour de France hadn't been dramatic enough in terms of the racing and results, the Tour de France Femmes came along and said 'hold my beer'. The start of the race was a bit of a slowburn, admittedly, but as we arrived in Nice for the final weekend, the temperature – both literal and metaphorical – was turned up to the max.

First was the bitter clash between Célia Gery and Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney , with the Polish rider angrily confronting Gery and accusing her of deliberately blocking her in order to benefit Demi Vollering, with something of a war of words ensuing over the next 24 hours. On top of that, Marlen Reusser suffered a nasty crash on the final stage that saw her tumble off the podium – after previously being in the lead and fighting for the win – and roll into Nice heartbroken and in tears.

And that's all without mentioning the race itself, which saw three different riders wear yellow over the final four days, with a battle for seconds right up until the final finish line in one of the most thrilling editions of the women's Tour we've seen yet. It was tense and sweltering under the Nice sun, and feelings definitely boiled over at times, which is why this goes down as one of the most dramatic weekends of the season.

Tadej Pogačar crashes out of the Vuelta

The second major GC crash-out of the season was even more dramatic that Vingegaard's. Pogačar is a rider who crashes relatively rarely, so to see him go head-over-handlebars, whilst in the red jersey and the overwhelming favourite to win the Vuelta a España, was shocking and almost unbelievable, so rare is such an incident. We think a small rock in the road was to blame for one of the worst crashes of Pogačar's career, and not just because it dramatically took away his chance of completing his Grand Tour set, but because he suffered some truly nasty injuries. He suffered a concussion, a fractured collarbone, and three fractured vertebrae, having to undergo surgery and a significant stay in hospital.

The crash changed the course of the Vuelta – Enric Mas soared to victory in the race that looked nailed-on for Pogačar – but also the whole rest of the season, with new faces coming to the fore at the World Championships, Euros and Il Lombardia, races which the Slovenian has previously dominated. In many ways, Pogačar's crash was the defining moment of the latter part of 2026, and a healthy dose of drama for the rider who often seems to glide right past any misfortune.

title: 'Ridiculous and stupid' – Mads Pedersen hits out at UCI contract rules which sees riders wearing old teams' kit to new team training camps
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
Mads Pedersen has hit out at the UCI contract rule requiring riders to wear their old kit at their new team's training camps.

This week, Primož Roglič and Richard Carapaz have been seen wearing Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe and EF Education-EasyPost kits as they met up with NSN for the first time, and in the coming weeks we'll see more and more of these out-of-place kits during teams' December camps.

It's all down to UCI regulations, which mean contracts run to December 31, meaning riders are still representing their 'old' teams until the New Year. Regulation 2.15.139 reads, 'The riders may not, for the duration of the present contract, work for any other team or advertise for any other sponsors…'

Speaking on his podcast, Pedersen called the regulation "ridiculous and stupid."

"You could simply include a clause stating that in the event of a team switch from December 1 – or from the first training camp – you are allowed to use your new team’s equipment," he said.

"That would make it so easy. Then you wouldn’t have all that nonsense anymore, and you would prevent riders from missing out on their pay in December because they were riding a Ridley while contractually they were required to ride a Trek."

Pedersen will witness a host of riders in their old team's kit when his Lidl-Trek team meet up in Spain next month. Key new signings Filippo Ganna, Felix Gall, and Jordan Jegat will be wearing Netcompany Ineos, Decathlon CMA CGM, and TotalEnergies kits.

"We are working on it with the AIGCP [the association of professional cycling teams] and the CPA riders' union," he said.

"The regulation change will definitely happen, with contracts starting on November 1. The starting year is yet to be determined in consultation with all stakeholders."

Riders and teams favour changing the rules, and the UCI was reportedly seeking to do so, yet the rules remain in place, drawing complaints from fans and the peloton.

title: Drivers over 70 face eye tests every three years under new plans
text:
Over-70s will have to take eye tests every three years or face losing their driving licence under new road safety plans.

Mandatory eyesight tests are part of the Department for Transport's (DfT) road safety strategy, expected within weeks.

Around 6.5 million over-70s hold drivers' licences, with 1.6 million of those aged 80 or over.

To drive legally in the UK, you must be able to read a standard number plate from 20 metres away, wearing glasses or contact lenses if required.

Government sources told the BBC ministers will recommend over-70s be made to regularly prove their eyesight meets the minimum standards. Those who do not, or who fail to meet the minimum standard face losing their licence.

The change follows a consultation which launched early last year , set to recommend a shake-up of the rules for older drivers.

Under the current rules, over 70s have to renew their licence every three years, but only have to self-certify that their sight.

Dennis Reed, of campaign group Silver Voices, which represents older people, said it was "discriminatory to just pick an age out of the hat and say 'everybody over 70 has to go through this, but nobody else does'".

But he said the group is not opposed in principle to regular eye tests for older drivers.

The changes being considered were first reported by the Daily Mail , external .

Drivers over 70 to face eye tests every three years

The NHS provides free eye tests for over 60s, but they are not detailed enough to approve someone to drive.

The BBC understands this system is also being looked at, with the free tests likely to be expanded to become more rigorous.

A Government source said "beefed up measures" were long overdue.

"One life lost on the roads is one too many," they added. "There have been several arguably preventable fatalities on Britain's roads caused by drivers with failing eyesight in recent years.

The DfT said no decision has officially been made on mandating eyesight tests for drivers aged 70 and over.

A spokesperson said: "We recognise the importance of driving for older people's independence but need to balance this with our priority to keep everyone safe on our roads and avoid tragic accidents.

"Mandatory eye tests for drivers over 70 as part of our Road Safety Strategy are one way to do this.

"We are carefully reviewing consultation results," they added. "Older drivers who are fit to drive and have good enough vision have nothing to worry about."

title: Primož Roglič tempted by each Grand Tour in 2027, but a decision is several weeks away
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
Primož Roglič has not yet made a decision on his race calendar for 2027, saying it was “way too early” given he only signed for his new team, NSN Cycling, little over a week ago. But he did say that all three of the Grand Tours are tempting him in their own way.

Roglič has won the Vuelta a España a joint-record four times, and he also has a Giro d’Italia title to his name from 2023, with the Tour de France the one missing from his palmarès.

Next year, the Giro d’Italia represents something of a draw, given the race heads into his native Slovenia, first on stage 1, then an entirely Slovenian stage the next day. The Tour de France, meanwhile, might represent some of that “unfinished business” he spoke about this week, especially after not racing it this year.

And the Vuelta of course is the Grand Tour where he has made his name and stands a chance of becoming the outright record holder with five titles, after showcasing his persisting Grand Tour credentials with the runner-up spot this year.

"Actually, we sat down together with the directors and a couple of guys, and then we started talking, you know," Roglič said during a first round of interviews from the NSN Cycling training camp in Spain this week.

"The Giro starts almost in Slovenia, the second stage is in Slovenia, the Zoncolan [on stage 20] is not far from Slovenia… nice.

"The Tour de France, I was not there last year. It’s missing me… nice.

"The Vuelta, you know… also nice."

Roglič has clearly started mulling things over but insisted no decision has been taken yet, saying he has other business to attend to first, namely meeting all his new teammates and staff, as well as familiarising himself with his new equipment.

"Later on, hopefully, yes, we start to make more seriously a deeper program, and from that, we can also define which Grand Tours I would like to do.

"We can also then make a [plan for the] start of the season, but for sure I will not start early in Australia or something like that."

NSN Cycling’s general manager Kjell Carlstrom also insisted it was too early to decide where Roglič will race in 2027, indicating that they will wait for the route for the Vuelta a España to be revealed on January 14.

"The other thing that we definitely want to see is the the Vuelta route and how that is designed because we believe that without knowing what the Grand Tours look like, it's impossible to build a complete calendar," Carlstrom told .

"Then you have to start from the Grand Tours and which ones it would be. Because I would presume that he has the capacity to do more than one, and on a good level. So we need to look at this carefully before we decide where he's going.

"We only spoke really with him yesterday in terms of getting to understand him better, what type of rider he really is, from the character perspective, and what he likes, what he doesn't like, and all these things, which are very important when you plan a calendar.

"Now the performance team needs to really take this into consideration and try to set down a draft plan of what it could look like."

While it’s too early to say where Roglič will race, the team have already confirmed a partial plan for their other star signing, Richard Carapaz, who is heading to the Giro d’Italia in May.

Carapaz will certainly race two Grand Tours in 2027 but at this point it has not been confirmed whether that will be the Tour or Vuelta, with that decision again likely to be made after the Vuelta route reveal, and in collaboration with Roglič's schedule.

Carapaz has confirmed his intention to target the GC at the Giro, with Carlstrom indicating he could opt for "differing goals" – ie stage wins – in his second Grand Tour of the year.

Carlstrom insisted the two riders could dovetail well, but Roglič spoke of “sharing the calendar” with his new teammate. That, and given another new climber signing, Santiago Buitrago, is also set for the Giro, would make it unlikely that Roglič heads to Italy in May, even with the draw of the Slovenian stages.

The Tour de France and Vuelta a España, then, would appear to be the logical combination.

title: ‘So Stupid’: Mads Pedersen Dumps on One of UCI’s Most Ridiculous Rules
author: Jim Cotton
text:
(Photo: Christine POUJOULAT / AFP via Getty Images)

You can always rely on Mads Pedersen to say it how it is.

In his latest quotebomb, the cobblestone bruiser slammed UCI registration rules, deeming them “fucking ridiculous.”

Speaking in this week’s episode of his Lang Distance podcast, Lidl-Trek’s verbose Dane blasted regulation that forces riders moving teams to black out their new equipment until January 1.

“It’s crazy with these contracts, isn’t it? Why don’t they just run from November 1 or December 1?” Pedersen said.

“It’s fucking ridiculous,” Pedersen raged. “It’s so stupid.”

Best not to ask Pedersen’s thoughts about the sock height rules, then.

UCI legislation requires rider contracts to align with the calendar year, rather than the racing season.

That means that riders who hook up with their new teams at December training camps must wear their outgoing employer’s kit. They can ride their new team bikes, as long as they’re debranded.

For example, Primož Roglič was recently spotted at the NSN Cycling winter get-together wearing a Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe jersey. The Slovenian was riding what was clearly an NSN-issued Cube bike, albeit with some hastily taped-over logos.

Pedersen suggested to podcast co-host Jakob Egholm that a simple paperwork tweak would fix the farcical off-season ritual.

“The contracts don’t have to be any different,” Pedersen said. “You can just add a clause to the contract saying that if you change teams, you’re allowed to use your new team’s equipment from December 1 or from the first team training camp.

“It would be so easy to change the contracts,” he said. “Then there wouldn’t be any bullshit or riders not getting their salary in December because they’ve ridden a Ridley when they were supposed to ride a Trek.”

Sergio Higuita famously got himself in hot water with EF Education-Nippo at the end of 2021 for this very same “ bullshit.”

The EF team threatened to “fire” the Colombian in the November of his final contract year, and so deny him some salary, after he was seen brazenly pedaling around on a Specialized bike supplied by his new team, Bora-Hansgrohe.

This commotion over contract dates crops up every off-season.

All it takes is a glimpse of a duct-taped bike logo to trigger a rider into a rage.

The continued backlash has prompted the UCI to promise that contract start dates will be officially moved from January 1 to November 1.

UCI director of sport Peter Van den Abeele said at the end of 2025 that such plans are in the works. However, the revised regulation has not yet been implemented.

Neville, Carragher and the inescapable podcasting feedback loop of doom | Jonathan Liew
author: Jonathan Liew
text:
Even the best managers can struggle to escape ex-players’ need to manufacture a crisis for content. Enter Michael Carrick …

A podcast studio in Manchester. A production runner pours water into jugs. Gary Neville enters the room with Michael Carrick.

Neville: Just so you know, we’re already filming. This is the intro bit, where we show everyone coming on to set and doing some light banter. It humanises us. The viewer sees it and thinks we’re just mates chatting about football, rather than scions of a global podcast empire commercially obliged to produce an endless scroll of provocative content for money. I always say: why can’t you be both?

Neville: Hang on, these Huel bottles need to be showing the label. Who’s turned the Huels round? Pathetic.

Jamie Carragher enters, followed by Roy Keane and Jill Scott.

Carragher: Salford failed to win at the weekend, Gary!

Neville: Yes, but banal observation about young James at Wigan!

Ian Wright enters, humming a Mary J Blige tune.

Neville: You’re watching Stick To Man United on The Overkill, with ManBank. Look, we all know there are times when you just want to bank with your mates, in a room, together. Download the ManBank app today. We’ve got a special guest today: the former manager of Manchester United Football Club, Michael Carrick. Now Carra, before we start …

Neville: The situation at United right now, it really hurts. I say that as a fan, I don’t use this word lightly, but it’s a real tragedy what’s happened to this football club. OK, you’ve got Grimsby and MK Dons. You’ve got the relegation in 1974. You’ve got Tommy Docherty leaving the club in disgrace. You’ve got Old Trafford being destroyed in a bombing raid during the second world war. You’ve got the very real threat of bankruptcy in the early 1900s. This, to me, is worse than any of that.

Carragher gazing at the ceiling : I always think about the great United teams under Sir Alex. Vidic. Ferdinand. Jaap Stam. Wes Brown. Patrice Evra. Even Denis Irwin, going back to Bruce and Pallister. You had Schmeichel in goal. You had Ince and Bryan Robson in midfield. You had Mark Hughes. You had Cantona. I look at the current side and think: do I see a Mark Hughes in there? Do I see a Cantona? And the answer is: only to an extent .

Neville: Roy, how do United move forward from this? They’ve got Brentford at the weekend.

Keane shrugging : Well, a team like Manchester United, you should always be beating a team like Brentford.

Neville: Yeah, but how do they go about it?

Keane: Well, the players in that dressing room, they need to be looking at themselves. And saying: come on, a team like Manchester United should always be beating a team like Brentford.

Neville: But tactically, what’s the plan?

Keane: If you keep asking me the same question, you’ll get the same answer, only louder.

Scott: I remember something Sarina was telling us at the Euros. We’d just beaten Norway and …

Neville: You take a look at that defence. Yoro. Mazraoui. Dalot. De Ligt. You can’t tell me there’s a worse defence in the history of professional football than those four. You put those four up in a park game, and it would be carnage. You choose any four inanimate objects – say a Kleenex, a butternut squash, a roof tile and a Belkin USB-C to Lightning charging cable – and they would do a better job in defence for Manchester United Football Club.

Carragher: Only thing making it worse is if you and Phil were playing in it!

Wright: Look, I see this United team now, which Roy played in, and Gary played in, and I just think: where’s the heart? Where’s the soul? It’s like they’ve lost something. And until they get it back … I don’t know. I just can’t feel it. I’m not feeling it.

Keane: But you talk about heart, and you talk about soul. These are international footballers ! It’s their job! I’m inexplicably furious about this point in particular!

Carragher: Let’s bring Michael into the discussion here, because you were dealt a tough hand, not just in terms of the recruitment, but the level of scrutiny around the club, around any big club, there’s a noise there. I remember talking to Daniel Agger about it. And Martin Skrtel. Steven Gerrard. Xabi Alonso. Dirk Kuyt.

Scott: There is that constant background chatter, though, isn’t there, at a club like United? I remember Sarina once telling us …

Neville: I remember, the gaffer – Sir Alex – once telling us that at United, a defeat is a disaster. Because of that constant background chatter. Because of how it would be perceived in the media. Did you feel like that constant judgment, whether it was from the media, or from fans, or from prominent ex-players, sometimes on podcasts: did you feel like that was creating extra problems for you?

Twenty-second ad for Manbrella, a precision-engineered umbrella made specifically to fit the male palm. Press Skip to return to video .

Neville: Did you feel like those ex-players in the media, players who had won trophies at United, but who now earn a living off talking about the club, almost preferred it when the club was failing? Because it gave them something to talk about? Because it made their own era look rosy in comparison? Because it did better numbers? And did that broader need to manufacture crisis, to paint every setback as if it was the worst disgrace in human history rather than the inevitable variance of a transitional team in a strong league labouring under an absentee ownership, create an inevitable doom spiral, an inescapable feedback loop from which even the very best managers have struggled to escape over the last 13 years?

Carragher: Sounds like you could be talking about yourself there, Gary!

title: What's gone wrong at Poundland?
text:
The future of Poundland hangs in the balance after the discount retailer's collapse into administration.

Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.

Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.

Its collapse puts the jobs of its 11,000 employees at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.

People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.

Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.

Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year.

According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor, "this isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland".

She told the BBC the tills were "busier than they were a year ago", adding that on the face of it a turnaround seemed "well under way".

However, Gordon Brothers had been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.

Poundland faced "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", according to Palmer.

However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams claimed the business was making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers painted a different picture, saying the chain remained "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

It said it had provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.

Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk

Poundland workers 'in limbo' over firm's future

It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.

As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1.

As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.

"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."

Irish firm Martin Property Group, London-based holding company Xyra Group and German investment firm Zachert Private Equity are all also understood to have made offers for Poundland.

Gordon Brothers had also been weighing options to break Poundland up.

Its view was that ultimately breaking the retailer up would provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate would also have to agree to keep the employees on.

Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale accuse it of driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.

But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim.

Now that the company has entered administration, consultants at Alix Partners have been appointed to pursue a sale of the business and its assets.

There are various options on the table, which include securing a buyer for the business either in whole or piecemeal.

The prime minister has said he wants "every effort made to secure a deal that protects jobs and keeps as many shops open as possible".

In the immediate future, Poundland stores and distribution centres will continue operating as normal.

title: The dhow builders crafting giant historic ships in India – in pictures
author: Frédéric Noy
text:
It takes three years for shipbuilders in the 16th-century port of Mandvi to complete a commission, in a trade that is as cultural as it is technical

I n the 16th century, the port city of Mandvi on India’s west coast was founded by the rulers of the kingdom of Kutch, and quickly established itself as one of the most dynamic ports in the western Indian Ocean. Its strategic geographical position, along the estuary of the Rukmavati River, which flows into the Arabian Sea in the Gulf of Kutch, and mastery of monsoon wind navigation enabled it to become part of vast maritime networks connecting India to the Gulf, the Arabian peninsula and east Africa.

Mandvi prospered through trade, exporting cotton textiles, indigo, cereals and handicrafts, while importing dates, pearls, Arabian horses and luxury goods.

The city was renowned for its shipyards, which specialised in building huge teak dhows suitable for long voyages across the Indian Ocean. This craft industry was a pillar of the local economy, contributing to Mandvi’s influence far beyond India, and it continues to employ many families of carpenters and other workers today.

It was from the 19th century onwards that Mandvi began to fall into economic decline. The advent of steamships, the need for deep, modern port infrastructure, and British colonial rule, which restructured maritime trade to serve its own interests, led to a shift in trade to better-equipped ports such as Mumbai.

After independence in 1947, the creation of the nearby port of Kandla definitively marginalised Mandvi commercially. Mandvi was also affected by the 2001 earthquake in Kutch, which damaged some of the old buildings and accelerated its urban transformation.

The city still clings to its few traditional shipyards, where workers from different religious communities build the boats. While a large proportion of them are Muslim, shipbuilding is also part of a very ancient Hindu tradition.

Each dhow takes several years to build by hand and employs about 25 craftsmen. Apprenticeships begin in adolescence, in a world where teams are related and the trade is as much cultural as it is technical.

Away from the shipbuilding, the city today is known for its neglected architectural heritage and its beaches, which attract Indian tourists and middle-class locals.

title: A vocal cohort of tech leaders celebrates Huang’s Nvidia return, but others are keeping quiet
author: Dara Kerr
text:
Elon Musk and Sam Altman among those rejoicing but Google, Meta and Apple chiefs have declined to weigh in

T he phrase “return of the king” rippled across social media on Monday. A vocal subsection of the tech industry was celebrating the resurrection of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s CEO. Some called him the “imperial and royal majesty”, others anointed him as “our Jesus” and several simply posted a crown emoji.

“The mistake has been corrected,” said Elon Musk. “Jensen!” exclaimed OpenAI’s Sam Altman.

It had been a whirlwind two weeks that started with the ouster of Huang as Nvidia’s CEO after his admission of an extramarital affair with a woman some in the US government feared to be a Chinese spy. Two more alleged affairs with company employees were later revealed. Silicon Valley engineers and venture capitalists decried Huang’s departure at the time, writing an open letter to Nvidia’s board of directors saying: “Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice.”

Donald Trump also got involved. The president repeatedly said that he’d like to see the return of Huang calling the CEO a “fine person” and “honorable guy”.

In the meantime, Nvidia’s stock tanked, falling more than 10%, and shedding hundreds of billions in value. Nvidia , which designs powerful computing chips used for artificial intelligence, is among the world’s top five most valuable companies.

On Monday, in a stunning reversal, Nvidia’s board unanimously voted to reinstate Huang. The decision came after Trump dialed into the company’s Sunday board meeting to advocate for Huang’s return. In a statement, the White House said: “We have to protect our geniuses.”

Nvidia’s stock rebounded, gaining nearly $1tn in market value. Trump, who owns shares in the chip maker, took a victory lap, making up to $15m with the surge on Monday.

Silicon Valley’s venture capitalists also rejoiced. Jason Calacanis, an angel investor, Nvidia stock-holder and co-host of the tech-centric All-In podcast, wrote a flurry of posts on X. He posted an AI image of a shining long-haired Huang depicted as Jesus holding a graphics processing unit (GPU) in place of the bible, writing : “GPU Jesus has risen.”

Other tech figures took the news personally. Travis Kalanick, the disgraced Uber CEO who was pushed out by his board, was one of the top figures fighting for Huang’s reinstatement. In past weeks, he frequently posted on X, saying “Bring Jensen back”, “LFG” (Let’s fucking go), and “We’ve got your back”.

Kalanick was reportedly among a small group of venture capitalists who lobbied Trump and JD Vance to push Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang, according to the FT . On Monday, Kalanick posted: “I will always sign up to serve him.”

While a vocal cohort of Silicon Valley insiders high-fived Huang’s return, it’s been radio silence from several other of the industry’s top leaders and rank-and-file workers.

The CEOs of Google, Meta and Apple have not weighed in on the debate. When Amazon’s Jeff Bezos was asked at an event last week if he thought Huang should be reinstated, he responded : “I don’t know enough of the details … so I can’t answer that question.” Microsoft’s Satya Nadella had a similar response.

Anil Dash, an entrepreneur with a career in leading smaller tech companies, is one of the few voices in tech who has publicly criticized Huang’s reinstatement. He says it sends the wrong message to the industry – that there are no rules, boundaries or accountability.

Dash pointed to widespread rationale for Huang’s return, which is based on the CEO being singularly crucial in the AI arms race against China. Calacanis, for example, has trumpeted this justification, saying : “We can not [sic] lose the race for super intelligence to China – period, full stop.”

And now, Dash said, Huang could have been compromised by a Chinese asset, and he’s running the biggest company in the industry. “It doesn’t make any sense,” he said. “We’re all being gaslit and we’re at a certain point where we’re like, ‘No, the sky’s not green. The sky’s blue.’”

Dash says the hundreds of thousands of tech workers who live in fear of being swept up in the increasingly frequent waves of layoffs, as the industry pivots to AI, aren’t able to speak up even if they disagree with Huang’s reinstatement. They don’t know if their “boss agrees with these guys”, Dash said.

Alison Taylor, an associate professor at New York University’s Stern Business School, said that mentality extends beyond Silicon Valley to the White House, given that Trump played a part in Huang’s return. “Trump’s whole thing is retaliation,” she noted.

“The message is: if you don’t shut up and go along with it, you’re not going to survive,” Taylor said. “It’s a fuck you to everybody who believes in the rule of law and who believes in anything being fair.”

Huang apologized to Nvidia staff in a company-wide meeting on Tuesday for “some terrible mistakes” he made. The CEO also rejected narratives that he was a “tech bro” who was “above the law”, adding it was “completely untrue” that Trump pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate him.

“Everything he’s done, it’s just his affection, his admiration, his recognition of the great company that you are,” Huang said of Trump.

In a separate statement , Huang thanked leaders across the industry for their “extraordinary support”.

“I can’t wait to get back to work,” he added.

title: Israel ‘officially sanctions’ torture of Palestinian prisoners to extract confessions, report concludes
author: Emma Graham-Harrison and Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem
text:
Public Committee Against Torture in Israel examined 42 complaints against Shin Bet interrogators over past decade

Israel has institutionalised the use of torture to extract confessions from Palestinian prisoners, sometimes documenting abuse in official records or granting advanced approval for “special measures” in interrogation, according to a report from the Public Committee Against Torture in Israel (PCATI).

This dangerous practice risked leading to irreversible miscarriages of justice, as Israel moved to implement a racist new death penalty law that targets Palestinians, the report said.

PCATI examined 42 cases in which Palestinians filed complaints about the use of torture by Shin Bet interrogators over the last decade.

More than three-quarters said they confessed after the use of “torture or other illegal methods”, and one in 10 provided incriminating statements about other people under torture.

“When it comes to Palestinian detainees, the Israeli legal system officially sanctions torture as a tool for extracting confessions, regardless of whether the content of those confessions is true,” said Sari Bashi, the executive director of PCATI.

“Torture as a tool of interrogation is particularly egregious given initiatives to impose the death penalty in Israel for the first time since 1962.”

Over the years, in hundreds of testimonies , Palestinian detainees have consistently described interrogations employing extreme sleep deprivation, physical violence such as slapping and kicking, threats, sexual violence and being held in stress positions.

Some of this abuse is also laid out in the official records of Shin Bet, Israel’s internal security service. PCATI details the case of a Palestinian lawyer arrested in February 2019 who was subjected to extreme sleep deprivation.

During an interrogation period lasting 27.5 days, or 660 hours, he was questioned for more than 552 hours, an average of 20 hours a day, with one session lasting nearly 48 hours. Some of the remaining 108 hours were spent travelling to and attending detention hearings.

In a 1999 ruling, Israel’s supreme court explicitly prohibited sleep deprivation as a deliberate interrogation method. Despite this, the lawyer was convicted of involvement in shooting attacks based on information extracted during this period.

The state inspector for complaints about Shin Bet interrogations (Mavtan) ruled that the interrogations took place in accordance with procedures, PCATI said.

More than 1,680 torture complaints were filed between 2001 and 2024 with Mavtan. None have led to an indictment.

Other cases are indirectly documented in Israeli judicial records, although judges rarely accept testimony about torture of Palestinians, PCATI said.

In one case, a detainee’s false confession, made under torture, was used as evidence by prosecutors. The man was released after his lawyer presented proof that he was not present at the scene of the crime, PCATI said.

Sleep deprivation was the most frequently used form of torture in complaints examined by PCATI, but more than half included the use of stress positions and other forms of physical violence.

Israel is a signatory to the UN convention against torture, but its legal system has effectively codified the use of violence and abuse where it is deemed “necessary” to extract life-saving information, PCATI said.

In a “necessity interrogation” or “military interrogation”, Shin Bet officials torture detainees “after consulting with their superiors and following an internal procedure for documenting their decisions and conduct”, the report said.

“[A] supposedly narrow exception ballooned and developed into a sprawling system of legal and administrative exceptions that swallowed the so-called rule, enabling the use of violence while maintaining the appearance of prohibition,” it continued.

There is no publicly available information on the scale of “necessity interrogations” inside the Shin Bet, PCATI said. They are an urgent concern as Israel moves to end a de facto moratorium on the death penalty, which had stood since the 1962 execution of the Nazi war criminal Adolf Eichmann.

“The death penalty is always wrong, because it’s cruel, irreversible and negates the right to life. No one should be executed, particularly not in a system tainted by systematic violence,” Bashi said.

In March, the Knesset passed a racist law allowing the execution of Palestinians convicted of terror charges over deadly attacks, but not Jewish Israelis who commit similar crimes.

In the occupied West Bank , where Palestinians are tried in military courts, execution is now the default punishment for a defendant found guilty of deadly terror attacks.

The legislation drew fierce international criticism, including from the UN’s high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, who warned that it would constitute a war crime if enacted.

A separate law empowers a special tribunal to impose death sentences in cases arising from the 7 October 2023 attacks.

Even in rare cases where courts have excluded confessions obtained under torture, Israeli case law allows prosecutors to use information derived from them as evidence to secure convictions.

PCATI said that as detention conditions worsened after October 2023, rights groups documented a sharp rise in violence by Israeli prison guards and soldiers , including beatings, attacks with dogs, electric shocks, threats and rape.

At least 103 Palestinian detainees have died in Israeli custody since 7 October 2023. Of 10 postmortems reviewed by Physicians for Human Rights Israel , five showed signs of physical assault and six showed evidence of medical neglect.

The Israel Prison Service said “all prisoners are held in accordance with the law”. The Shin Bet and Israel’s justice ministry did not respond to requests for comment.

title: Car finance compensation payments explained
text:
Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements could face further delays to compensation after the financial regulator said it had made some errors in its calculations.

Driver have already been told they must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, although some may be offered an early settlement.

Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).

However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed.

The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest.

Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024.

The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period.

In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them.

The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much.

Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan.

Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders.

Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of £829 per mis-sold agreement.

The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit £9.1bn.

How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered.

The FCA has announced some claimants might be offered an early settlement, but only if it as good as what would be paid under the current proposed central scheme.

Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything.

The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company.

The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts.

Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation .

The FCA has published this guidance on how to complain , external .

lenders will respond to claims, explaining if you are owed compensation and how much – but timing of those letters is now uncertain owing to the legal challenge

those who complain before the scheme gets up and running are likely to receive compensation faster

some people who complained by 30 June and are not owed compensation should be told by 18 November, if the agreement began on or after 1 April 2014 and you complained by 30 June 2026

some of those who complained by 31 August will be told if they are not owed compensation by 18 January 2027, if the agreement began before 1 April 2014

there are exemptions , external , and anyone who does not hear from their lender by the dates set out, isn't necessarily owed compensation

those who have not complained will be contacted by their lender. People will be asked if they want to opt in to the scheme to have their case reviewed

those motor finance borrowers who do not receive a letter - for example because lenders no longer have their details and cannot trace them - can still make a claim

Regulators have warned claims management companies and law firms involved in motor finance commission claims to make sure consumers do not have multiple representatives for the same claim and are not charged excessive termination fees.

FCA boss Nikhil Rathi told the BBC's Today programme there are "many law firms out there who would like to get 30% of any compensation", stressing that the regulator's scheme was "free to use" for consumers.

Millions of drivers were in line to receive compensation this year, and most of the remainder should have got compensation by the end of 2027.

But the FCA has confirmed that no compensation will be paid before 2027 as a result of legal challenges to the scheme.

The watchdog has now said it uncovered some mistakes in how it categorised a small group of loan agreements under its redress scheme, which could have a small impact on compensation levels.

"While the potential impact on average compensation is small – less than £10 per agreement, on average – we recognise this affects the ongoing litigation," the FCA said. That could leave average payouts somewhere between £819 and £839.

"We will discuss with the challengers and the court the impact on this deadline, and for the timeline of the litigation."

Consumer Voice has said the scheme leaves "too many people short-changed" . The FCA has also received challenges from three lenders: Volkswagen Financial Services, Mercedes Benz Financial Services, and Credit Agricole Auto Finance.

The UK's Upper Tribunal has agreed to hear legal challenges to the scheme, with a hearing scheduled for 16 February to 3 March.

It means that lenders will no longer need to calculate or pay compensation to people owed money under its scheme, until the legal process concludes.

The FCA said it would need to decide what to do next if the courts decided to overturn the programme. Without a scheme in place, the FCA has estimated that up to 19 million complaints would need to be handled individually, taking three years and costing lenders £6bn more.…

title: Bearman to continue with Haas in 2027
text:
Britain's Oliver Bearman will continue to race for the Haas team in Formula 1 in 2027.

The US-based team announced the 21-year-old's new deal on Thursday, at the start of the Qatar Grand Prix weekend.

It marks Bearman's third full season with Haas, for whom he first raced for two one-off events in 2024 before becoming a full-time driver in 2025.

The announcement ends a protracted negotiation period in which Bearman's management were seeking reassurances about his future from Ferrari.

Bearman is a member of the Italian team's driver academy and has ambitions to race for Ferrari in the future.

It was not immediately clear what reassurances Bearman had been given about his future by Ferrari.

Is Hamilton and Leclerc's Ferrari partnership sustainable? F1 Q&A

Camara to continue with Haas for final two races

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu said: "Continuing with Ollie into 2027 was a natural decision for us.

"We've seen his growth, his commitment, and the quality he brings to the team, both on and off the track.

"He has a tremendous work ethic and a strong desire to develop both himself and the team, and there is no better person, in my opinion, to lead this team forward."

Bearman added: "It's no secret that I'm delighted to be continuing with Haas into 2027.

"This team has played an integral role in my development, and I've felt a huge amount of belief and support from everyone here.

"We've got big ambitions to keep pushing forward, and I'm excited to lead that work, building on what we've achieved, and striving for even more together – we have unfinished business."

Bearman will be partnered at Haas next season with Brazilian Rafael Camara, who is also a member of the Ferrari driver academy.

Camara has started racing for Haas at the end of this season, following the team's sacking of Frenchman Esteban Ocon midway through the Mexico City Grand Prix weekend.

Bearman's concerns about his future had been rooted in the fact that there might not be a seat available at Ferrari for some considerable time.

Charles Leclerc is on a long-term contract there, and while Lewis Hamilton's deal is believed to end after 2027, the seven-time champion is keen to continue in F1 for a number more years.

Bearman, who said at last weekend's Las Vegas Grand Prix, that he was "quite disappointed" his new contract had not yet been sorted so late in the season, is believed to have been exploring his options.

His management is said to have been asking Ferrari for reassurances about his future, either about the possibility of racing for the main team, or if that is not an option, being allowed to pursue a career at a more competitive team than Haas.

title: Musk's plan to send a million SpaceX data satellites into space approved
text:
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.

The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.

Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".

"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.

Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.

The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.

Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).

Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation—one that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.

The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.

Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.

Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

title: ‘It’s Not Going to Be Just Sole Leadership’: Quinn Simmons Campaigns for Tour of Flanders
author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
text:
Quinn Simmons is angling to ride the Tour of Flanders, the American champion revealed to Velo .

After years of avoiding the cobbled classics, a return to the Belgian monument would be a shake-up for Simmons, who has gravitated towards the hillier monuments in recent years.

It would also be a shake-up for the Lidl-Trek classics squad, with Simmons dropping into a team that has been built around getting Mads Pedersen a monument victory for the better part of the last decade.

It would also be the first time that Simmons has ridden Flanders since his debut in 2022, when he didn’t finish.

“My first objective of the year will be Flanders,” Simmons told Velo in an exclusive interview in Tucson, Arizona. “I still haven’t got the full confirmation that I can go, but in my head that is the first goal.”

The shift in program for Simmons stems from two separate but equally important developments from the 2026 season for the 25-year-old all-rounder.

“When I basically gifted Mads [Pedersen] a Tour stage this year, I think that was when the team started to realize that maybe there’s going to be some changes. For next year, it’s not going to be just sole leadership,” Simmons said.

“If that’s hard for him to accept, that’s how it is. For sure, he’s one of the best riders in the world, but now, with the team we have, we can’t only be putting eight guys around one anymore,” he continued.

“I think it’s not just for myself, but for the other riders we have on the team like [Mathias] Vacek and some other guys coming up. If we go into the monuments, you have to play with two cards. Pogačar, Van der Poel, and Van Aert—they’re too good to only beat with one. We’re gonna need to adapt that plan a bit.”

That confidence was gained not just through the Tour, where Simmons was a frequent attacking and pulling presence, but also through a successful one-day race campaign to end the year.

The high point was the Team USA win at the UCI World Championships with Brandon McNulty, but that was part of a bigger picture where Simmons showed his form throughout the Canadian, Italian, and Japanese races on his program.

He also has Remco Evenepoel as an example of how parachuting into Flanders can fit into a larger calendar.

“It came from how I was racing the one-day races at the end of the year,” Simmons said. “With the way Remco did it, where you do Catalonia first and then go to Flanders, I think it can work. If I can do an altitude block and then come to Flanders quite in good shape.

“If I have to be in Belgium the four weeks before, I just don’t believe I can maintain the form that I need that long, but I think if I can climb with a similar level to Worlds, I believe Flanders has at least the potential for something to happen.”

Simmons began his career as a highly touted classics prospect but quickly moved away from the cobblestones and toward the hill classics and the Tour de France.

While a return won’t change his ultimate goal of a Tour stage win, it does add another chance for Simmons and his Lidl-Trek team to win the big monument they have been lacking.

“If I can be there in the same role there, that’s how Mads [Pedersen] can win—if we go there together,” he said. “Hopefully that gets approved, and if not, then I’ll just do my normal program of going to Basque, Amstel, and then preparing for the Tour.”
